stem: Scenario of migraine with aura in a 70 years old lady H/O hypothyroidism induced constipation Prophylaxis?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Patient has migraine with aura
•
Also has a history of hypothyroidism
• The question asks for the most appropriate prophylactic (preventive) treatment
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Propranolol):
•
Propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker, is first-line prophylaxis for migraine with or
without aura.
•
It reduces the frequency and severity of migraine attacks by:
o
Modulating vascular tone
o
Inhibiting adrenergic activation
•
It is safe and effective in patients with hypothyroidism, as long as bradycardia is not present.
• It is the most established and evidence-based option among those listed for migraine
prevention.
Why Other Options Are Less Suitable:
Option Reason It’s Less Suitable
Amitriptyline
Effective for migraine prophylaxis, especially if coexisting depression or poor sleep.
However, not first-line, and has anticholinergic side effects that may be poorly
tolerated in some, especially older patients.
Gabapentin Occasionally used off-label for migraines, but limited evidence; not first-line.
Sumatriptan
This is for acute treatment, not prophylaxis. Also contraindicated in some cases of
migraine with aura due to slight vasoconstrictive stroke risk.
Aspirin
Not effective for migraine prophylaxis; may help in mild tension headaches, but not
suitable here.
Summary:
For a patient with migraine with aura and hypothyroidism, propranolol is the most appropriate and
well-established preventive treatment.
Correct answer: Propranolol
.
A 53 years old with 1 year H/O excessive blinking more when stressed / tired.
Vision affected.
H/O HTN being treated on ramipril
O/E: Hardening / stiffening / contracture of “orbicularis muscle ’
Neurological and fundus exam is normal.
Most likely diagnosis?
Facial tick
Ocular myasthenia
Ocular blepharospasm
Post blepharitis
Facial myokymia
ANSWERS:
Ocular blepharospasm
Correct answer: Ocular blepharospasm
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Age: 53 years old
•
Symptoms:
o
1-year history of excessive blinking, worsens with stress and fatigue
o
Affects vision
• Examination:
o
Contracture/stiffening of orbicularis oculi muscle
•
Neurological and fundus exams are normal
•
No signs suggestive of systemic neuromuscular disease
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Ocular blepharospasm):
• Blepharospasm is a focal dystonia involving involuntary, repetitive, forceful contraction of
the orbicularis oculi muscle
Symptoms include:
o
Excessive blinking, eye closure, and visual impairment due to difficulty keeping eyes
open
o Worsens with stress and fatigue, which is characteristic
•
Examination may reveal orbicularis oculi hardening or stiffness due to chronic overuse/spasm
•
It is not related to structural eye pathology, and neuro/fundus exams are normal
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
Option Why It’s Incorrect
Facial tic
Tics are brief, intermittent, suppressible movements; often include other facial
muscles and don’t cause muscle stiffening or affect vision this way.
Ocular
myasthenia
Causes fatigable weakness, not spasms; usually shows ptosis, diplopia, and worsens
with sustained gaze, not blinking.
Post-
blepharitis
Blepharitis causes irritation, redness, and crusting of eyelids, but not involuntary
muscle contractions or spasms.
Facial
myokymia
Involves fine rippling/twitching of facial muscles (especially orbicularis oculi), not
sustained spasms or contractures. Usually transient, not disabling.
Summary:
This patient has classic features of ocular blepharospasm — a chronic, involuntary contraction of the
orbicularis oculi muscle, especially worsened by fatigue or stress, with vision interference.
Correct answer: Ocular blepharospasm.

stem: 72 year old male with metastatic lung cancer. Agitated & distressed with severe pain. Pain is controlled with morphine and cyclizine pump. Which further medication is suitable to control his agitation?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Patient: 72-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer
•
Current issue: Agitation, despite pain now being well controlled with morphine and cyclizine
via syringe driver
•
Question focuses on managing agitation, not uncontrolled pain
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Midazolam):
•
Midazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine, widely used in palliative and end-of-life care for:
o
Agitation
o
Anxiety
o
Terminal restlessness/delirium
•
It can be given subcutaneously, often via the same syringe driver already being used for
morphine and cyclizine.
•
It provides calmness and comfort, making it the first-line treatment for agitation in terminal
patients.
Why Other Options Are Less Appropriate:
Option Why It’s Not Suitable in This Case
Glycopyrronium
Anticholinergic used to manage excess respiratory secretions, not
agitation.
Increased morphine dose
Pain is already controlled. Increasing morphine may oversedate or
cause respiratory depression unnecessarily.
Hyoscine (butylbromide or
hydrobromide)
Used for noisy respiratory secretions (death rattle); can actually
worsen confusion or delirium.
Levomepromazine
Can be used for agitation but is more sedating and typically reserved
for when midazolam is ineffective or contraindicated.
Summary:
In this palliative care scenario, agitation with controlled pain is best managed with midazolam, the
safest and most effective first-line sedative for terminal restlessness.
Correct answer: Midazolam.
In palliative care, compatibility between drugs in a syringe driver is crucial — particularly when
combining multiple agents like cyclizine and midazolam.
Cyclizine + Midazolam in Syringe Driver: Compatibility Issues
•
Cyclizine is incompatible with many other drugs when mixed in a single syringe driver.
•
Cyclizine and midazolam are generally incompatible when mixed in the same syringe driver
solution.
o
The mixture often results in precipitation or cloudiness, indicating chemical
incompatibility.
o
This can lead to clogged lines, reduced drug delivery, or local irritation.
Recommended Practice:
If you want to give midazolam for agitation alongside cyclizine and morphine:
1. Do NOT mix midazolam in the same syringe driver as cyclizine.
Use a separate subcutaneous line (butterfly cannula) for intermittent or continuous midazolam
administration.
o
Example: Subcutaneous bolus 2.5–5 mg every 2–4 hours PRN, or
o Start a second syringe driver for continuous infusion if agitation is persistent.
Compatible Drug Combinations:
• Morphine + Midazolam → generally compatible
•
Morphine + Cyclizine → often used together, although cyclizine is relatively irritant and can
crystallize if diluted improperly
• Midazolam + Cyclizine → not reliably compatible
Summary:
Cyclizine and midazolam should not be mixed in the same syringe driver due to incompatibility risks. If
both are needed, use separate subcutaneous sites or drivers.

stem: 29 year old pregnant lady presented with breathlessness. A diagnosis of pulmonary embolism was made in the 8th week of pregnancy. What is the treatment until peripartum period?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Patient: 29-year-old pregnant woman, diagnosed with pulmonary embolism (PE)
•
Timing: At 8 weeks gestation (1st trimester)
• The question asks for the appropriate treatment until the peripartum period
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Low Molecular Weight Heparin):
•
LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin) is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy for conditions like PE or
DVT.
•
It is:
o
Safe in pregnancy (does not cross the placenta)
o Has predictable pharmacokinetics
o
Requires less monitoring than unfractionated heparin
•
Treatment is typically continued throughout pregnancy and into the postpartum period
(usually up to 6 weeks postpartum)
•
In the peripartum period, LMWH may be switched to unfractionated heparin closer to delivery
(due to shorter half-life), but LMWH remains the mainstay throughout pregnancy.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
Option Why It's Incorrect
Aspirin Antiplatelet, not anticoagulant; ineffective for treating PE
IV Unfractionated
Heparin
Used acutely if immediate reversal needed (e.g., in unstable patients), but not
practical for long-term outpatient management
SC Unfractionated
Heparin
Safe but requires frequent dosing and monitoring; LMWH preferred due to
ease of use and better bioavailability
Warfarin
Contraindicated in pregnancy, especially 1st trimester, due to teratogenicity
and risk of fetal bleeding (crosses placenta)
Summary:
In a pregnant woman with PE, low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is the safest and most effective
long-term treatment up to the peripartum period.
Correct answer: Low molecular weight heparin
A COPD patient presents with SOB, tachycardia, tachypnea and chest pain.
Pulmonary embolism is suspected.
Which is best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
USG
D-dimer
CTPA
Chest Xray
VQ scan
ANSWERS:
CTPA
Correct answer: CTPA (CT Pulmonary Angiography)
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Known COPD patient
•
Presents with sudden onset shortness of breath, tachycardia, tachypnea, and chest pain
• These are classic signs of pulmonary embolism (PE)
•
Question asks for the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis
Explanation of the Correct Answer (CTPA):
•
CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the gold standard and first-line imaging for diagnosing
pulmonary embolism in most stable patients.
•
It allows:
o
Direct visualization of thrombi in the pulmonary arteries
o
Evaluation of alternative diagnoses (e.g., pneumonia, pneumothorax)
•
Especially important in COPD patients, where chest symptoms may have multiple possible
causes, CTPA offers high sensitivity and specificity
Why Other Options Are Less Suitable:
Option Why It's Less Appropriate
USG (leg
Doppler)
Used to detect DVT, which supports PE diagnosis, but does not confirm PE itself. Only
used if CTPA is contraindicated or unavailable.
D-dimer
Useful to exclude PE in low-risk patients, but this patient is high-risk (classic symptoms
• COPD). D-dimer is nonspecific and likely to be elevated in COPD, infections,
inflammation.
Chest X-ray
Often normal in PE or may show non-specific changes; helpful to rule out other causes
(e.g. pneumothorax, consolidation) but not diagnostic for PE
V/Q scan
Can diagnose PE, especially in patients with contraindications to contrast (e.g., renal
failure, allergy). But less useful in COPD due to underlying lung changes that often
result in non-diagnostic or indeterminate scans. CTPA is preferred in COPD.
Summary:
For a COPD patient with suspected PE, CT pulmonary angiography is the most accurate and
definitive test to confirm the diagnosis.
Correct answer: CTPA.

stem: 45 y/o male H/O travelling presented with 5 day history of fever with abdominal pain, Abdomen is tender; but no signs of peritonism Febrile presently, but stable currently Blood culture: Salmonella typhi Stool culture: negative Already taking ciprofloxacin What is the next best treatment option?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
• 45-year-old male with recent travel
•
Fever for 5 days + abdominal pain, tender abdomen
•
Blood culture positive for Salmonella typhi
•
Stool culture negative (common early in illness)
•
Currently on ciprofloxacin, but still febrile
•
Now needs a decision on next step in management
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Switch to Ceftriaxone):
•
Persistent fever despite ciprofloxacin suggests antibiotic resistance, which is increasingly
common in S. typhi, especially in travel-associated cases, particularly from South Asia.
•
Multidrug-resistant (MDR) and fluoroquinolone-resistant Salmonella typhi strains are now
prevalent in many endemic areas.
•
Ceftriaxone (a third-generation cephalosporin) is:
o
Highly effective against Salmonella typhi, especially in resistant strains
o
First-line IV treatment in moderate to severe or resistant typhoid fever
• Because the patient remains febrile despite ciprofloxacin, this implies treatment failure, and
escalation to a more effective agent like ceftriaxone is appropriate.
Why Other Options Are Less Appropriate:
Option Reason It's Incorrect
A) Continue ciprofloxacin
and observe
Not appropriate — the patient has confirmed bacteremia and is still
febrile after several days → implies treatment failure/resistance
B) Add gentamicin
Gentamicin has poor intracellular penetration, and S. typhi is an
intracellular pathogen; not effective
C) Add metronidazole
Targets anaerobes, not appropriate for treating Salmonella, which is a
facultative intracellular aerobe
E) Switch to
chloramphenicol
An older treatment for typhoid, now rarely used due to bone marrow
suppression, resistance, and availability of better alternatives like
ceftriaxone
Summary:
In a patient with confirmed typhoid fever and failure of ciprofloxacin, the best next step is to switch
to ceftriaxone, which is effective against fluoroquinolone-resistant Salmonella typhi.
Correct answer: D) Switch to Ceftriaxone.

stem: Middle aged man with MI 4 months ago. On Ramipril, Aspirin, Atorvastatin, Clopidogrel. Came with facial swelling of sudden onset. Which drug is responsible?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
• Middle-aged man with myocardial infarction 4 months ago
•
On Ramipril, Aspirin, Atorvastatin, Clopidogrel
•
Presents with sudden-onset facial swelling (suggestive of angioedema)
•
The question asks which drug is responsible
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Ramipril):
• Ramipril is an ACE inhibitor, and a well-known cause of angioedema
•
ACE inhibitors:
o
Increase bradykinin levels (by inhibiting its breakdown)
o Bradykinin accumulation causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability,
leading to angioedema
•
This can occur any time after starting the drug — not limited to the early days
•
Facial swelling, especially of the lips, tongue, or airway, is typical
•
There is no associated urticaria or itching, distinguishing it from allergic reactions
Why Other Drugs Are Less Likely:
Drug Reason It's Less Likely
Aspirin
Can cause hypersensitivity reactions, but not classic for isolated angioedema; usually
involves urticaria, bronchospasm
Clopidogrel Rarely causes skin reactions, but not a known common cause of angioedema
Atorvastatin Can cause muscle symptoms or liver issues, not angioedema
ACE inhibitors like Ramipril are the most likely cause of sudden-onset angioedema, even months
after starting.
Correct answer: Ramipril.

stem: CKD patient with Polycystic kidney disease presented with bone pain & CKD with BP 120/80. Labs showed Hypocalcemia (2.10 mmol) and hyperphosphatemia (2.80 mmol). What is cause of hyperphosphatemia?
options: Vit D Deficiency / Decrease levels of cholecalciferol
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
CKD patient (with polycystic kidney disease)
•
Presents with:
o
Bone pain
o Hypocalcemia (2.10 mmol/L)
o
Hyperphosphatemia (2.80 mmol/L)
o
BP normal (120/80) — suggests patient is stable
• Likely represents CKD-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD)
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Decreased phosphate excretion):
• In chronic kidney disease, especially stages 3–5, the kidneys lose the ability to excrete
phosphate effectively
As GFR declines:
o
Phosphate clearance falls
o
Serum phosphate levels rise → hyperphosphatemia
• This triggers:
o
Secondary hyperparathyroidism (as PTH is stimulated to try to excrete more phosphate
and maintain calcium)
o
Suppression of 1-α-hydroxylase, reducing active vitamin D → contributing to
hypocalcemia
• The primary mechanism of hyperphosphatemia in CKD is the impaired renal excretion of
phosphate.
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
Option Why It's Incorrect
1. Increased phosphate
reabsorption
In CKD, the kidneys lose excretory function, not due to increased
reabsorption. PTH tries to reduce reabsorption, not increase it.
2. Enzyme defect
Not relevant here — no specific enzyme defect is responsible for
hyperphosphatemia in CKD.
3. Hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a consequence of
hyperphosphatemia, not the cause. PTH aims to decrease phosphate.
4. Vitamin D deficiency
Leads to hypocalcemia, but not directly to hyperphosphatemia. The
phosphate retention is due to impaired renal excretion, not vitamin D
deficiency.
Summary:
In CKD, hyperphosphatemia is primarily caused by decreased renal excretion of phosphate due to
declining GFR.
Correct answer: 2. Decreased phosphate excretion
Right sided Bell's palsy.
Which of the following features support the diagnosis of Bell's Palsy?
1. Hyperacusis
2. Hyperaesthesia
3. Hyperlacrimation
4. Hypersalivation
5. Hyperhidrosis
ANSWERS:
Hyperacusis
Correct answer: 1. Hyperacusis
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Right-sided Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral, lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve palsy
of unknown cause (often viral, e.g., HSV)
•
The question asks: Which associated symptom supports the diagnosis?
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Hyperacusis):
•
Bell’s palsy involves the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), which has multiple branches and
functions:
o
Motor to facial muscles
o
Parasympathetic fibers to lacrimal and salivary glands
o
Taste to anterior 2/3 of the tongue
o
Motor branch to stapedius muscle in the middle ear
•
In Bell's palsy, when the nerve is affected proximal to the stapedius branch, there is paralysis
of the stapedius muscle, which normally dampens sound.
o
This results in hyperacusis (sounds seem abnormally loud) on the affected side
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
Option Explanation
2. Hyperaesthesia
Not typical in Bell’s palsy; sensory nerves of the face are from the trigeminal nerve
(CN V)
3.
Hyperlacrimation
Bell's palsy more commonly causes reduced lacrimation due to parasympathetic
involvement. Sometimes reflex lacrimation increases due to poor drainage, but it's
not a classic or supportive feature.
4. Hypersalivation
Bell’s palsy may lead to reduced salivation, not increase. Drooling may occur due to
poor lip closure, but that’s mechanical, not increased production.
5. Hyperhidrosis
Sweating is under sympathetic control, not facial nerve function; unrelated to Bell’s
palsy.
Summary:
Hyperacusis is a classic supportive feature of Bell’s palsy, caused by facial nerve involvement proximal
to the stapedius muscle branch.
Correct answer: 1. Hyperacusis.

stem: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome. What is the mode of inheritance?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Autosomal Dominant (AD)
Explanation:
• Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome is an autosomal dominant inherited cancer syndrome.
•
It is caused by a mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 3p25-26.
•
Because it’s autosomal dominant, only one copy of the mutated gene is sufficient to increase
cancer risk.
•
There is a 50% chance of passing it on to offspring if one parent carries the mutation.
Key Features of VHL Syndrome:
System Manifestation
CNS Hemangioblastomas (cerebellum, spinal cord)
Eyes Retinal angiomas
Kidneys Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell type)
Adrenals Pheochromocytoma
Pancreas Cysts, neuroendocrine tumors
Epididymis / Broad ligament Papillary cystadenomas
Clinical Pearl:
▪ Always suspect VHL syndrome in a young patient with bilateral renal cell carcinoma, CNS
hemangioblastomas, or a family history of similar tumors — and remember its autosomal
dominant inheritance
Dad with Marfan syndrome
Wife is normal
Percentage of children being affected?
ANSWERS:
50%
Correct Answer: 50% of children will be affected
Explanation:
• Marfan syndrome is inherited in an Autosomal Dominant (AD) pattern.
•
This means:
o
Only one copy of the mutated gene (from either parent) is enough to cause the disease.
o An affected individual (like the father) has genotype M/m (M = mutant, m = normal).
o
A normal individual (like the mother) has genotype m/m.
Punnett Square Outcome (Father M/m × Mother m/m):
m (mother) m (mother)
M (dad) M/m → Affected M/m → Affected
m (dad) m/m → Normal m/m → Normal
Result:
• 50% chance of child being affected (M/m)
•
50% chance of child being unaffected (m/m)
In autosomal dominant conditions like Marfan syndrome, each child of an affected parent has
a 50% chance of inheriting the disorder, regardless of sex.

stem: A patient had pheochromocytoma. His mother had medullary thyroid cancer (suggesting MEN2A). What is the probability of passing this condition to his children?
explanation:
Correct Answer: 50%
Explanation:
•
Both pheochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) are hallmark features of
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) — especially MEN2A.
•
MEN2 is inherited in an Autosomal Dominant (AD) pattern.
•
This means that:
o
Only one copy of the mutated RET proto-oncogene is needed to cause the syndrome.
o An affected individual (e.g., the patient with pheochromocytoma) has one mutant RET
allele (RET⁺/RET⁻).
o
When this patient has children with someone without the mutation (RET⁻/RET⁻), there’s
a: 50% chance the mutation will be passed to each child
Clinical Genetics Pearl:
•
In Autosomal Dominant conditions like MEN2:
o The mutation is inherited in a vertical pattern (one affected parent → child).
o
Each child of an affected individual has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutated gene.
o
RET genetic testing is crucial for affected families — even in asymptomatic relatives.

stem: A patient presents to ED with raised BP, HR, RR, and massively elevated CK. Most likely cause?
explanation:
Correct Answer: MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine) toxicity
Key Clinical Clues:
•
Raised BP, HR, and RR → Sympathetic overactivity
•
CK massively elevated (↑↑↑↑) → Suggests rhabdomyolysis
•
Presentation is consistent with a toxic or drug-induced hyperadrenergic state
Explanation of the Correct Answer (MDMA):
•
MDMA (ecstasy) is a synthetic amphetamine derivative that increases:
o
Serotonin
o
Dopamine
o
Norepinephrine
•
Classic features of MDMA toxicity:
o
Hyperthermia
o Agitation, anxiety
o
Tachycardia, hypertension
o
Sweating, tremors
o
Hyponatremia (due to SIADH or excessive water intake)
o
Severe rhabdomyolysis → markedly raised CK, risk of AKI
o
May lead to seizures, DIC, or multi-organ failure
Differentials and Why They Are Less Likely:
Cocaine: Similar hyperadrenergic state, but CK is usually less extreme unless prolonged agitation
or seizures occur.
•
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): Causes high CK but typically in the setting of
antipsychotic use, with rigidity and altered mental status.
•
Serotonin syndrome: May overlap but more commonly associated with SSRIs + other
serotonergic drugs; clonus, hyperreflexia more prominent.
•
Malignant hyperthermia: Associated with anesthesia, not street drugs.
Clinical Pearl:
MDMA toxicity = Sympathetic overdrive + hyperthermia + rhabdomyolysis (↑↑↑ CK)
Early recognition is critical to prevent renal failure and death

stem: A 56 year old female treated for pneumonia with amoxicillin and clarithromycin, 5 days later she developed AKI Eosinophil count: elevated 2.0x 10
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
56-year-old woman recently treated for pneumonia
•
Received amoxicillin and clarithromycin
• Developed acute kidney injury (AKI) 5 days later
•
Eosinophil count is elevated (2.0 × 10⁹/L)
Explanation of the Correct Answer (AIN – Acute Interstitial Nephritis):
•
Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is a common cause of AKI due to a hypersensitivity reaction,
often to drugs.
•
Classic triggering drugs:
o
Beta-lactam antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin)
o
Macrolides (e.g., clarithromycin) can also contribute
o NSAIDs, PPIs, diuretics, etc.
•
Typical triad (seen in <10% but useful when present):
6. Fever
7. Rash
8. Eosinophilia
•
In this case:
o
Recent drug exposure
o
Eosinophilia
o AKI developing days after starting antibiotics
→ Strongly supports AIN
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
Option Why It's Incorrect
1. Eosinophilic granulomatosis
with polyangiitis (EGPA)
Would present with asthma, sinusitis, pulmonary infiltrates,
neuropathy, and positive ANCA. Not seen here.
2. Microscopic polyangiitis
A pauci-immune small-vessel vasculitis that causes rapidly
progressive GN, usually ANCA positive, with hematuria and
proteinuria. No supporting features here.
3. Post-streptococcal
glomerulonephritis (PSGN)
Occurs 1–3 weeks after strep throat or skin infection, presents
with hematuria, edema, hypertension, not eosinophilia or recent
drug use.
4. IgA nephropathy
Typically follows mucosal infection (e.g., URTI), and presents with
hematuria, not eosinophilia. AKI is not common unless there's
rapidly progressive GN.
Summary:
In a patient who developed AKI days after starting antibiotics, especially with eosinophilia, the most
likely cause is acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) — a drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction.
Correct answer: 3. AIN.

stem: 28 year old, recurrent vomiting for 1 year, visits the gym regularly, hx of 3 drug overdoses in the past. He believes he was overweight. He made regular visit to the gym BM1 20kg/m2. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
28-year-old
•
Recurrent vomiting for 1 year
• BMI = 20 kg/m² (normal range)
•
Regular gym activity
•
History of 3 drug overdoses (suggests emotional dysregulation or impulsivity)
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Bulimia Nervosa):
•
Bulimia nervosa is characterized by:
o Recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors such as
vomiting, excessive exercise, or laxative use
o
Normal or near-normal body weight (unlike anorexia)
o
Often associated with impulsivity, emotional instability, and self-harming behavior,
including overdose
•
This patient:
o
Is vomiting recurrently
o
Has a normal BMI (20) — ruling out anorexia nervosa
o Goes to the gym regularly, possibly as a form of compensation
o
Has a psychiatric history of overdoses — fits the impulsive/affective pattern seen in
bulimia
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
Option Why It's Incorrect
1. Body dysmorphic
disorder
Involves preoccupation with imagined flaws in appearance, but not
associated with vomiting or purging
2. Anorexia nervosa
Requires BMI <17.5 or significant underweight + restrictive eating or
purging; not met here (BMI 20)
3. Borderline personality
disorder
May explain impulsivity and overdose, but doesn't directly cause
recurrent vomiting or focus on body image/eating
4. Delusional disorder Involves fixed false beliefs, unrelated to eating behaviors or vomiting
Summary:
A patient with recurrent vomiting, normal BMI, compensatory exercise, and impulsivity/overdoses
fits the pattern of bulimia nervosa.
Correct answer: 3. Bulimia nervosa.

stem: 17 year old Female, corneal clouding on examination, optic nerve normal, Hx of hurler syndrome: alpha-L- iduronidase deficiency. In which organelle are hydrolases found?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
• 17-year-old female with Hurler syndrome
•
Caused by α-L-iduronidase deficiency
•
Clinical sign: Corneal clouding
• Question asks: Where are hydrolases (like α-L-iduronidase) located?
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Lysosomes):
Hurler syndrome (MPS I) is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of α-L-
iduronidase, an enzyme needed to degrade glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) like heparan sulfate
and dermatan sulfate.
• This enzyme is a type of acid hydrolase, which functions optimally in the acidic environment of
the lysosome.
•
Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing digestive enzymes (hydrolases) that
break down:
o
Cellular waste
o Complex macromolecules
o
Damaged organelles
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
Organelle Reason It's Incorrect
1. Mitochondria Involved in energy production, not degradation via hydrolases
2. Endoplasmic
reticulum
Involved in protein synthesis/folding and lipid metabolism, not degradation
3. Ribosomes Involved in protein synthesis, not enzyme-mediated degradation
4. Vacuoles
Mostly relevant in plant cells; in animal cells, their role is not equivalent to
lysosomal function
Summary:
Hydrolases like α-L-iduronidase are found in lysosomes, which are responsible for intracellular
degradation.
Correct answer: 3. Lysosomes.

stem: A 48 years old man with H/O clarithromycin treatment 6 weeks ago,13 units alcohol / week consumption. H/O fatigue AMA = 1:640 Anti-smooth muscle ab normal GGT increased Dx?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
48-year-old man
•
Past clarithromycin use (6 weeks ago) – possible but not definitive for DILI
•
Alcohol intake: 13 units/week → moderate, not enough for alcoholic liver disease
•
AMA (anti-mitochondrial antibody): 1:640 – strongly positive
•
Anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA): abnormal but not the primary finding
•
GGT elevated – marker of cholestasis
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Primary Biliary Cholangitis – PBC):
•
PBC is a chronic autoimmune cholestatic liver disease involving destruction of intrahepatic
bile ducts.
•
Diagnostic features include:
o
Strongly positive AMA (present in >90% of cases)
o Cholestatic liver enzymes: Elevated ALP and GGT
o
More common in women, but can occur in men
The high AMA titre (1:640) is diagnostic of PBC in the appropriate clinical context, even if other
antibodies like ASMA are also present.
While ASMA is associated with autoimmune hepatitis (AIH), a strongly positive AMA overrides this in
favor of PBC.
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
Option Why It’s Incorrect
2. Alcoholic Liver Disease
(ALD)
Alcohol intake is modest (13 units/week); ALD typically shows AST>ALT,
no AMA positivity
3. Autoimmune Hepatitis
(AIH)
ASMA is seen in AIH, but AMA is not; AIH usually has hepatocellular
pattern (↑ALT/AST)
4. Drug-Induced Liver
Injury (DILI)
Clarithromycin can cause cholestasis, but DILI typically does not
produce AMA positivity; also DILI is more acute
5. Primary Sclerosing
Cholangitis (PSC)
Associated with IBD, more common in young men, usually has p-ANCA
positivity, not AMA
Summary:
The very high AMA titre, cholestatic pattern, and absence of other overriding causes make Primary
Biliary Cholangitis the most likely diagnosis.
Correct answer: 1. PBC.

stem: A patient presents with brief episodes of vertigo triggered by head position changes. Dix-Hallpike test is positive. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario (Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo - BPPV):
•
BPPV is characterized by:
o
Sudden, brief episodes of vertigo
o Triggered by changes in head position (e.g., turning in bed, looking up)
o
No hearing loss or tinnitus (helps differentiate from Ménière’s)
o
Caused by dislodged otoliths (canaliths) in the posterior semicircular canal
Management: Epley Maneuver
•
The Epley maneuver is a canalith repositioning procedure used to treat posterior canal BPPV.
•
It involves a sequence of head and body movements that move the dislodged otoliths from the
semicircular canal back into the utricle, where they no longer cause symptoms.
•
It is a first-line, non-pharmacological, effective treatment.
Patients often experience immediate relief or improvement after a single treatment.
Summary:
In Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV), the Epley maneuver is the recommended first-line
treatment to reposition displaced canaliths and relieve symptoms.
Correct answer: Epley maneuver.

stem: An old female came GP HR = 58 b/min + asymptomatic ECG: Complete heart block What would you expect to found in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:
In complete heart block (third-degree AV block):
•
The atria and ventricles contract independently (AV dissociation).
• This disruption in timing between atrial and ventricular contractions affects:
o
The intensity of the first heart sound (S1).
Why?
•
The first heart sound (S1) is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves.
•
The intensity of S1 depends on the position of the AV valves at the time of ventricular
contraction.
• Since atrial and ventricular contractions are unsynchronized in complete heart block:
o
Sometimes the ventricles contract just after the atria — producing a loud S1
Other times, the timing is off — resulting in a soft S1.
•
Hence, you get variable intensity of S1 — a classic auscultatory feature of complete heart block.
Why the other options are less correct:
Option Why It’s Less Likely
1. Low BP
BP may be normal if the escape rhythm is sufficient, especially in an
asymptomatic patient
2. Bradycardia
While present (HR = 58), it’s already provided in the question — the examiner is
likely testing for clinical auscultation findings
3. Giant V wave Seen in tricuspid regurgitation, not in heart block
4. Widely
variable S2
Not a typical finding in complete heart block; S2 is usually unchanged unless there's
valve pathology
Final Summary:
The classic auscultation finding in complete heart block is variable intensity of the first heart sound
(S1) due to AV dissociation.
Correct answer: 5. Variable intensity of S1.

stem: G protein couple receptor are found where?
explanation:
Explanation:
•
G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are a large family of cell surface receptors.
•
They are embedded in the cell membrane and are responsible for detecting extracellular signals
(e.g., hormones, neurotransmitters).
•
Upon ligand binding, GPCRs activate intracellular G proteins, which then trigger various second
messenger pathways (e.g., cAMP, IP₃/DAG).
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
Location Why Incorrect for GPCRs
Nucleus
GPCRs do not function inside the nucleus; nuclear receptors (e.g., steroid hormone
receptors) operate there
Mitochondria
GPCRs are not located in mitochondria; mitochondrial signaling uses other receptor
systems
Summary:
G protein-coupled receptors are located on the cell membrane, where they mediate signal
transduction from extracellular ligands.
Correct answer: Cell membrane
Gram negative bacteria scenario leading to Septic shock
Mechanism via which gram negative may lead to septic shock??
a) Exotoxin
b) Lipopolysaccharide
c) Protein A
d) Mucin
ANSWERS:
Lipopolysaccharide
Correct answer: b) Lipopolysaccharide
Explanation:
•
Gram-negative bacteria have a characteristic outer membrane that contains
lipopolysaccharide (LPS), also known as endotoxin.
•
LPS is a potent activator of the immune system and plays a central role in the pathogenesis of
septic shock caused by gram-negative infections.
Mechanism:
1. LPS is released during bacterial lysis or division.
2. It binds to TLR4 (Toll-like receptor 4) on macrophages and other immune cells.
3. This triggers a massive release of proinflammatory cytokines:
o
TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, etc.
4. Leads to:
o
Widespread vasodilation
o Increased capillary permeability
o
Hypotension
o
Multi-organ failure → septic shock
Why Exotoxin is Incorrect:
•
Exotoxins are secreted proteins produced mainly by gram-positive bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus
pyogenes, Clostridium tetani).
While some gram-negative bacteria can also produce exotoxins, LPS is the key mediator in
gram-negative septic shock.
Summary:
Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is the primary endotoxin in gram-negative bacteria, and it is responsible for
triggering septic shock through massive cytokine activation.
Correct answer: b) Lipopolysaccharide.

stem: 70 years old presented with lethargy. Examination showed splenomegaly Investigation showed Hb = 8.9 Platelet = 62 Normal White cell count Blood picture: Tear drop cells Diagnosis?
explanation:
Key features from the case:
• Age: 70 years — typical for myeloproliferative disorders.
Symptoms: Lethargy — common in anemia.
•
Examination: Splenomegaly — often massive in myelofibrosis due to extramedullary
hematopoiesis.
• Bloods:
o
Hb = 8.9 (anemia)
o
Platelets = 62 (thrombocytopenia)
o
Normal WCC (ruling out leukocytosis seen in CML)
•
Blood film: Tear drop cells (classic feature of myelofibrosis)
Why Myelofibrosis is the correct diagnosis:
•
Tear drop poikilocytes (dacrocytes) are highly characteristic of bone marrow fibrosis, where
distorted red cells are squeezed out of a fibrotic marrow.
•
They are classically associated with myelofibrosis, a type of chronic myeloproliferative
disorder.
•
Splenomegaly results from extramedullary sites (like the spleen and liver) and are often
deformed as they squeeze out of fibrotic marrow or abnormal sites — giving them a teardrop
shape.
• Pancytopenia (anemia + thrombocytopenia) supports marrow failure.
Why not CML:
•
CML usually presents with:
o
Marked leukocytosis
o
Basophilia
o
Splenomegaly (yes), but tear drop cells are not typical.
•
The normal WCC essentially rules this out.
Why not Multiple Myeloma:
• Multiple myeloma presents with:
o
Hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, bone pain/lesions (CRAB)
o
Rouleaux formation on blood film, not tear drop cells
o
Splenomegaly is not a typical finding
•
Platelets are usually normal unless very advanced.
Why not Vomiting:
•
Vomiting can occur with raised ICP but is:
o
Non-specific — also seen in gastroenteritis, pregnancy, and many other conditions.
o
Often early and less specific, especially in children.
•
It may be an initial symptom but not the most important or critical feature when suspecting or
diagnosing raised ICP in acute or emergency settings.
Conclusion:
In the context of suspected raised ICP, bradycardia is a more important and specific sign, often
reflecting impending brain herniation and requiring urgent intervention.

stem: Etanercept Molecular level action?
explanation:
Key clinical findings:
•
Progressive motor weakness in right hand (3 months)
• No sensory involvement — suggests a motor-only lesion
•
Wasting of:
o
Thenar eminence (median nerve territory)
o
Dorsal interossei (ulnar nerve territory)
•
Hypothenar sparing — interesting, but not exclusive
•
No pain — argues against entrapment neuropathies or radiculopathy
Analysis of findings:
This is a motor-only, progressive, and multifocal pattern involving both median and ulnar-innervated
muscles, which points to a lesion proximal to the peripheral nerves, but not involving sensory
pathways.
Why the answer is: Anterior horn cells
The anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons in the spinal cord) give rise to all motor innervation
to the limbs.
•
In diseases like motor neurone disease (MND / ALS):
o There’s painless, progressive weakness
o
Mixed UMN and LMN signs, but early signs can be LMN only
o
No sensory loss
o
Often starts asymmetrically in the hands
•
Muscle wasting and weakness affecting multiple nerve territories without sensory loss is classic.
Why not the others:
•
b. Brachial Plexus injury – would affect motor and sensory fibers; also usually painful and
traumatic in onset.
•
c. Cervical spinal cord – would affect motor and sensory, possibly with UMN signs below the
lesion.
•
d. Median nerve – would cause thenar wasting but not interossei.
•
e. Ulnar nerve – would cause interossei and hypothenar wasting, not thenar.
Conclusion:
The pattern of painless, motor-only wasting in multiple nerve distributions without sensory loss is
classic for anterior horn cell disease, most likely an early presentation of motor neurone disease (ALS).

stem: A 16 year old boy with 2 months of proximal muscle weakness, 1 month of dysphagia, rash over chest and back with violaceous discolouration of eyelids. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
• Age: 16-year-old male — dermatomyositis can occur in both children (juvenile dermatomyositis)
Proximal muscle weakness for 2 months — hallmark of inflammatory myopathies.
•
Dysphagia — suggests involvement of pharyngeal/upper esophageal muscles.
•
Skin findings:
o Violaceous rash over knees and knuckles — Gottron’s papules, pathognomonic.
o
Rash over chest and back — "Shawl sign" or "V-sign" common in dermatomyositis.
Why Dermatomyositis is correct:
•
It is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin findings and proximal
muscle weakness.
• Common skin signs:
o
Gottron's papules – violaceous plaques over knuckles, elbows, knees
o
Heliotrope rash – violaceous discoloration around eyes
o
Shawl sign/V-sign – rash over upper chest/shoulders
•
Dysphagia may occur due to pharyngeal muscle involvement.
Why not the others:
•
1. SLE:
o
Rash is typically malar (butterfly rash), photosensitive, and spares knuckles.
o
Muscle weakness is not a predominant early feature.
o
Rash over knuckles is more characteristic of dermatomyositis (not SLE).
•
2. Lichen planus:
o
Characterized by pruritic, purple, polygonal papules — usually affects wrists, ankles,
and mucosa.
o
No muscle weakness or dysphagia associated.
Conclusion:
The combination of proximal muscle weakness, dysphagia, and pathognomonic skin findings
(violaceous rash over knuckles, knees, and chest) is classic for dermatomyositis, making Option 3 the
correct diagnosis.

stem: A 58 years old woman with T2DM on metformin, Drinks 15 units alcohol per week. Hepatomegaly (6 cm) Weight 35 (BMI) kg/m O/E: mild Tenderness over Right upper quadrant. No Jaundice. Serum ferritin 420 S. ALT 150 Serum ALP 200 PT 11.0 USG abdomen: Bright echogenicity over Liver parenchyma & 2 stones on gallbladder No features suggesting CLD Dx?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
•
58-year-old woman with:
• Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)
•
BMI = 35 kg/m² → Obese
•
15 units alcohol/week → below the threshold for alcoholic liver disease (usually >35 units/week
in females)
•
Hepatomegaly + mild RUQ tenderness
•
Liver enzymes:
o
ALT = 150 (↑ → hepatocellular pattern)
o
ALP = 200 (mildly ↑)
• Serum ferritin = 420 → modestly elevated, acute phase reactant; not diagnostic of iron overload
•
PT normal, no jaundice, no signs of CLD
USG: Bright echogenic liver (suggests fatty liver), gallstones present
Why the answer is NASH (Metabolic steatohepatitis):
•
Patient has metabolic syndrome features:
o
T2DM
o
Obesity (BMI 35)
o
Mild hepatomegaly and tenderness
o Elevated ALT > AST (typical in NASH)
•
Ultrasound shows bright echogenic liver → suggests hepatic steatosis
•
ALT is markedly raised → indicates steatohepatitis (not just simple steatosis)
• Ferritin mildly elevated — common in metabolic syndrome due to inflammation (not
hemochromatosis)
•
Gallstones are likely incidental here, as they don’t cause hepatocellular enzyme elevation
without biliary obstruction
Why not the others:
• A) Alcohol: 15 units/week is not enough to cause alcoholic hepatitis; plus, in alcoholic liver
disease AST > ALT (typically AST:ALT > 2)
•
B) Gallstone: RUQ tenderness and gallstones, yes, but ALT 150 and echogenic liver point toward
liver pathology; no signs of cholecystitis or cholestasis
•
C) Hemochromatosis: Ferritin 420 alone is non-specific; in hereditary hemochromatosis, ferritin
is usually much higher (often >1000), transferrin saturation is key for diagnosis (not provided)
•
E) Metformin: Does not cause hepatotoxicity; in fact, it's protective in NAFLD/NASH and safe in
mild-moderate liver dysfunction
Conclusion:
This is a classic case of Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH) in a woman with T2DM, obesity,
elevated ALT, and fatty liver on ultrasound, making option D the most likely diagnosis.

stem: A 45 yr old woman presented with history of right elbow pain made worse by lifting. On examination, she had tenderness over the attachment of the wrist extensor at her elbow. The symptom reproduced by resisted wrist extension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
•
Pain over lateral elbow
•
Worse with lifting – especially with extended wrist
•
Tenderness over the attachment of wrist extensors – lateral epicondyle
•
Pain reproduced with resisted wrist extension – classic diagnostic maneuver
Why is Lateral Epicondylitis ("Tennis Elbow"):
•
Involves overuse injury to the common extensor origin, particularly the extensor carpi radialis
brevis (ECRB).
•
Classically presents with:
o
Pain/tenderness over the lateral epicondyle
o
Worse with gripping, lifting, or resisted wrist extension
o
Common in middle-aged adults and those with repetitive arm/wrist use
Why not the others:
•
6. Biceps tendinopathy: pain more anteriorly, near the bicipital groove or at the distal biceps
tendon, not lateral elbow.
•
7. Medial epicondylitis ("Golfer’s elbow"): affects flexor-pronator group with tenderness over
medial epicondyle; pain is provoked by resisted wrist flexion, not extension.
•
8. Olecranon bursitis: presents with swelling over posterior elbow, not localized lateral
tenderness or pain on wrist movement.
9. Triceps tendinopathy: pain is located posteriorly, near triceps insertion at olecranon, not
lateral side or with wrist extension.
Conclusion:
This is a classic presentation of lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), due to repetitive strain on the wrist
extensors, especially ECRB, with pain over the lateral epicondyle and on resisted wrist extension.

stem: Action of reverse transcriptase?
explanation:
What is Reverse Transcriptase?
•
Reverse transcriptase is an enzyme used by retroviruses (e.g., HIV).
• It synthesizes complementary DNA (cDNA) from an RNA template.
Normal flow of genetic information (Central Dogma):
• DNA → RNA → Protein
Reverse transcription (by reverse transcriptase):
• RNA → DNA
So:
•
Generation of DNA from RNA → Correct
• Generation of RNA from DNA → This is done by RNA polymerase, not reverse transcriptase.
•
DNA amplification → Done by DNA polymerase in PCR, not reverse transcriptase.
Clinical application:
•
Reverse transcriptase is crucial in:
o
Retroviral replication (e.g., HIV)
o
Molecular biology (e.g., creating cDNA from mRNA for RT-PCR)

stem: 31 year old came with feeling lethargic and ring size bigger. Known acromegaly, started on pegvisomant. M/A pegvisomant?
explanation:
Key facts about Pegvisomant:
Pegvisomant is a growth hormone (GH) receptor antagonist.
•
It is used in the treatment of acromegaly, particularly when:
o Surgery and/or somatostatin analogues are not effective or not tolerated.
o
GH levels remain elevated, and IGF-1 remains high despite treatment.
Mechanism of Action:
•
Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor on target tissues.
•
This prevents GH from exerting its effect, leading to a reduction in IGF-1 production by the
liver.
•
Unlike somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant does not inhibit GH secretion, but blocks its
action at the receptor level.
Why the other options are incorrect:
Option Explanation
1. Dopamine agonist E.g., cabergoline — sometimes used in acromegaly but not pegvisomant
2. Dopaminergic
antagonist
Not used in acromegaly and not relevant here
3. Somatostatin analogue
E.g., octreotide, lanreotide — these inhibit GH secretion, but pegvisomant
is not one
4. Somatostatin antagonist Not a recognized class used in acromegaly
5. GH receptor
antagonist
Correct — this is exactly what pegvisomant is
Conclusion:
Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist, used to reduce IGF-1 levels in acromegaly by blocking the
action of GH at its receptor.
Rt facial palsy. Inability to close eye
No other findings
Rx?
Aspirin
Acyclovir
Prednisolone
Prednisolone and aciclovir
ANSWERS:
Prednisolone
Correct answer: Prednisolone
Key clinical features:
•
Right-sided facial palsy
• Inability to close eye
•
No other neurological findings → suggests isolated lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy
(Bell’s palsy)
Best treatment: Prednisolone (alone)
•
Bell’s palsy is an idiopathic LMN facial nerve palsy
•
Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone) are proven to:
o
Improve recovery
o
Maximize chance of full resolution if started within 72 hours
Option Reason it’s incorrect
Aspirin No role in isolated Bell’s palsy
Acyclovir alone Antivirals alone are not effective; steroids are key
Prednisolone +
Acyclovir
Combination may help in severe or complete paralysis, but not superior to
steroids alone in mild/moderate Bell’s palsy; guidelines recommend steroids
alone in most cases
Conclusion:
For isolated LMN facial palsy (Bell’s palsy) with no other findings, the most appropriate treatment is
oral prednisolone, ideally started within 72 hours of symptom onset.

stem: One patient with type 2 DM with horizontal diplopia worsening over evening. Visual acuity and pupils are normal + unable to abduct eyes Orbicularis oculi muscle weakness What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Key clinical features:
•
Type 2 diabetes mellitus – may be relevant, but the rest of the features are more suggestive of
another condition.
•
Horizontal diplopia worsening as the day progresses – classic for fatigability, strongly
suggests myasthenia gravis.
•
Normal visual acuity and pupils – argues against cranial nerve palsies like 3rd or 6th nerve.
•
Bilateral inability to abduct eyes – suggests weakness of lateral recti, not a single CN VI palsy.
• Orbicularis oculi weakness – indicates extraocular muscle + facial muscle involvement,
characteristic of MG.
Why the answer is Myasthenia Gravis:
•
MG affects the neuromuscular junction, leading to:
o
Fatigable weakness
o
Often starts with ocular symptoms: ptosis, diplopia (due to variable EOM weakness)
o
Facial muscle involvement (e.g., orbicularis oculi) is also common
o
Pupils are not affected (key differentiator from other neurological causes)
Why the other options are less likely:
Option Why it's incorrect
2. DM
Diabetic cranial mononeuropathy can cause isolated CN III or VI palsy, but not bilateral
fatigable eye movement + facial weakness
3. 3rd nerve
palsy
Would involve ptosis and/or pupil involvement, and classically causes down and out
eye, not bilateral abduction failure
4. 6th nerve
palsy
Causes unilateral inability to abduct, not bilateral or fluctuating; also no orbicularis
oculi involvement
5. MS
May cause diplopia, but not fatigability or isolated orbicularis weakness; less likely
without other CNS signs
The combination of fatigable horizontal diplopia, bilateral abduction deficit, orbicularis oculi
weakness, and normal pupils and acuity is classic for Myasthenia Gravis.

stem: A 41 year old presented with nasopharyngeal tumour Causative organism?
explanation:
Key fact:
• Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is strongly associated with Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV),
particularly the non-keratinizing and undifferentiated subtypes.
Why EBV is correct:
•
EBV is a herpesvirus that:
o
Infects epithelial cells and B lymphocytes
o
Is linked to several cancers:
▪ Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
▪
Burkitt lymphoma
▪
Hodgkin lymphoma
▪ Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD)
•
EBV DNA and anti-EBV antibodies are often found in patients with NPC
Virus Reason it's incorrect
JC virus
Associated with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in
immunosuppressed patients, not NPC
HPV (Human
papillomavirus)
Associated with oropharyngeal cancers (especially tonsillar and base of
tongue), not nasopharynx
Conclusion:
The most likely causative organism in nasopharyngeal carcinoma is EBV (Epstein–Barr Virus).

stem: 30 years lady have developed facial hairs since last 6 months and irregular cycles, gained wait 8 to 10 kg . Have hirsutism and also showed glycosuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Key clinical features:
•
30-year-old woman
• New facial hair growth (hirsutism)
•
Irregular menstrual cycles
•
Weight gain (8–10 kg)
• Glycosuria – suggests insulin resistance or hyperglycemia
Why PCOS is the most likely diagnosis:
PCOS is a common endocrine disorder in reproductive-aged women, characterized by:
•
Hyperandrogenism → hirsutism, acne, alopecia
•
Ovulatory dysfunction → irregular cycles, infertility
• Insulin resistance → obesity, glycosuria, increased risk of T2DM
•
Weight gain is common and worsens insulin resistance and androgen excess
The combination of:
•
Hirsutism
•
Irregular cycles
•
Weight gain
•
Signs of insulin resistance (glycosuria)
→ strongly supports PCOS as the unifying diagnosis.
Why not the others:
Option Why it’s less likely
A) Adrenocortical
tumor
Can cause hirsutism, but usually with rapid onset, more severe virilization
(deep voice, clitoromegaly), and often Cushingoid features
B) Hemochromatosis
Rare in premenopausal women; typically causes diabetes, liver disease, skin
pigmentation, but not hirsutism or irregular cycles
Conclusion:
The constellation of hirsutism, irregular menses, weight gain, and insulin resistance is classic for
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS).

stem: 18 years old boy presented with facial swelling and have raised rash on his body there and hoarseness and stridor, tongue swelling. These developed after eating at a restaurant. He has no previous history. After ABCD assessment, what is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Key features of the scenario:
18-year-old male
•
Sudden onset after eating → suggests allergic reaction
•
Facial swelling, raised rash (urticaria), hoarseness, stridor, tongue swelling
→ These are classic signs of anaphylaxis
•
No prior history is irrelevant — anaphylaxis can occur on first known exposure
Diagnosis: Acute Anaphylaxis
•
Life-threatening allergic reaction involving:
o
Airway compromise (stridor, tongue swelling, hoarseness)
o Circulatory symptoms or rapid onset mucocutaneous symptoms
First-line, life-saving treatment:
•
Intramuscular (IM) adrenaline (epinephrine), 0.5 mg in adults (0.01 mg/kg in children)
o
Given into anterolateral thigh
o
Immediate action on:
▪ Reversing airway obstruction
▪
Raising blood pressure
▪
Reducing mucosal edema and bronchospasm
Why the other options are incorrect:
Option Reason
B) IV
Hydrocortisone
Steroids may help reduce recurrence, but have delayed onset (4–6 hours); not
life-saving in acute phase
C) Chlorpromazine Antipsychotic — no role in anaphylaxis
D) Adrenaline
infusion
Used in refractory or persistent hypotension after IM doses and fluid
resuscitation — not first-line
This patient is experiencing anaphylaxis, and the most appropriate immediate management after
ABCD assessment is Intramuscular Adrenaline — the first-line, life-saving treatment.

stem: 28 year old man Presented in a coma & in deteriorated condition. Methaemoglobin > 70% What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
•
28-year-old man in coma with deteriorating condition
•
Methaemoglobin >70% — very high and life-threatening
o
Normal levels: <1%
o
20%: symptoms
o 70%: coma, death likely without urgent treatment
Pathophysiology:
•
Methaemoglobinaemia: Hemoglobin is oxidized to Fe³⁺ (ferric) state → cannot bind oxygen
•
Leads to:
o
Severe hypoxia, despite normal PaO₂
o Cyanosis, dyspnea, altered consciousness, coma
Why Methylthioninium chloride (Methylene Blue) is correct:
• First-line antidote for symptomatic or severe methaemoglobinaemia
•
Acts as a reducing agent, converting Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺
•
Rapid onset of action
•
Given IV, usually 1–2 mg/kg
Why other options are less appropriate:
Option Reason it’s incorrect
Ascorbic acid
Weak reducing agent, used in mild cases or G6PD deficiency; too slow for life-
threatening levels
Ventilation Supportive, but doesn’t correct oxygen delivery defect caused by methaemoglobin
Hyperbaric
oxygen
No proven benefit in methaemoglobinaemia; more useful in CO poisoning or gas
embolism
High flow
oxygen
Helpful, but insufficient alone when methaemoglobin >70%; doesn’t reverse
oxidized Hb
Conclusion:
In life-threatening methaemoglobinaemia (>70%), the most appropriate and urgent treatment is
Methylthioninium chloride (Methylene Blue) — it directly reverses the cause of hypoxia.

stem: Patient with breathlessness: Low FEV1 (2.4L), Low FVC (4.8L), reduced TLCO, increased lung volumes. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Key Pulmonary Function Test (PFT) findings:
Parameter Value Interpretation
FEV1 Low (2.4 L) Obstruction
FVC Low (4.8 L) Possibly due to air trapping
FEV1/FVC ratio Reduced Confirms obstructive pattern
TLCO Reduced Impaired gas exchange
Lung volume Increased Suggests air trapping
TLC Increased Classic in emphysema
Why Emphysema is the correct answer:
•
Obstructive pattern (↓FEV1/FVC)
•
Reduced TLCO – due to destruction of alveolar walls, decreasing surface area for gas exchange
• Increased lung volumes & TLC – due to air trapping and hyperinflation
These are hallmark features of emphysema, a subtype of COPD involving destruction of lung
parenchyma.
Why not the others:
Option Why it's incorrect
1. Asthma
Also obstructive, but TLCO is normal or increased, and lung parenchyma is
preserved
2. Kyphoscoliosis Restrictive defect → ↓TLC, ↓lung volumes, not increased TLC
3. Pulmonary
fibrosis
Restrictive + reduced TLCO, but TLC is decreased, not increased
Conclusion:
This patient has an obstructive ventilatory defect with reduced gas transfer and hyperinflation,
which is most consistent with Emphysema.

stem: A mid 20 pt with smoking history came with persistent small productive cough with breathlessness. On examination he has coarse monophasic wheeze on left side of chest. FEV1 1.5 L FVC 2.5 L Chest x ray normal Next step?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
•
Young adult (~mid-20s)
• Smoker
•
Persistent small, productive cough + breathlessness
•
Unilateral coarse monophasic wheeze (left-sided) → suggests localized airway obstruction
• FEV1 = 1.5 L, FVC = 2.5 L → FEV1/FVC = 60% → obstructive pattern
•
Chest X-ray = normal → but does not rule out endobronchial pathology
Interpretation:
•
Monophasic wheeze on one side strongly suggests localized airway obstruction, likely
mechanical (e.g., endobronchial lesion, mucus plug, foreign body, or tumor).
• Obstructive spirometry pattern with no radiological abnormality further points to a central
airway lesion.
•
Normal CXR does not exclude an obstructive lesion in proximal airways, which can only be seen
endoscopically.
Why Bronchoscopy is the best next step:
• Monophasic wheeze on one side strongly indicates fixed obstruction (e.g., endobronchial
tumor, foreign body, mucus plug)
•
In a young smoker, one must consider endobronchial neoplasms (e.g., carcinoid) or post-
infective/mucus-related obstruction.
Bronchoscopy →
▪ Allows direct visualization of airways
▪ Can identify:
• Endobronchial tumors (e.g., carcinoid)
• Foreign bodies
Localized strictures or inflammation
▪ Can perform biopsy, aspiration, or therapeutic clearance if needed
Why not the other options:
Option Why it's inappropriate here
Peak flow rate
Non-specific; useful in asthma monitoring, not for suspected localized
obstruction
Salbutamol
reversibility test
Useful for asthma/COPD diagnosis, but not appropriate when there's a unilateral
wheeze with suspicion of localized lesion — could delay essential
bronchoscopy
CT scan chest
May show subtle lesions but bronchoscopy is superior for endobronchial
visualization and biopsy
A1 Anti-Trypsin
Relevant for early-onset panacinar emphysema, but not helpful for localized
wheeze or structural obstruction
Conclusion:
In a young smoker with a unilateral coarse monophasic wheeze with obstructive spirometry and
normal CXR suggests a central airway lesion. The most appropriate next investigation is Bronchoscopy
for direct airway assessment.

stem: Anderson Fabry male 34 yrs, wife no disease, 6 months pregnant, carrying male child. Risk of transmission of disease to the child?
explanation:
Key genetic background:
•
Anderson-Fabry disease is an X-linked recessive disorder.
• Affected male (XY) has the disease → his only X chromosome is mutated.
•
Wife is unaffected (not a carrier) → contributes a normal X or a Y.
•
They are having a male child (i.e., XY).
How inheritance works in this case:
•
Father always passes his Y chromosome to sons.
•
The X chromosome (which carries the disease) is passed only to daughters.
So:
•
Son inherits Y from father (not the affected X).
• Son inherits normal X from mother → but since he’s a boy, he doesn’t get the X — he gets Y
from dad and X from mom.
NOW:
▪ Since the child is male, and dad can only pass on his Y,
▪ The child cannot inherit the X-linked Fabry gene from his father.
Therefore: the risk of transmission to a male child from an affected father is:
0% — or effectively <1%
So the correct answer should be: 1. <1%
Summary:
•
Affected male with X-linked recessive condition (Fabry)
Non-carrier mother
•
Male fetus
•
Dad gives Y to son → no disease transmission
• Risk to male fetus = <1%

stem: Patient accidentally swallowed elemental mercury from a thermometer. What is the management?
explanation:
Key fact:
•
The mercury in a glass thermometer is elemental mercury, which is:
o
Poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract
o
Largely inert if swallowed (as opposed to inhaled vapor)
Clinical management of swallowed elemental mercury:
•
Accidental ingestion of elemental mercury (as in a thermometer):
o
Does not cause significant systemic toxicity
o
Most of it passes through the gut unchanged
•
Key concern is broken glass — risk of GI tract injury, not mercury toxicity
Why Observation is correct:
•
No chelation, decontamination, or dialysis is needed for swallowed elemental mercury
• Just observe for signs of:
o
GI perforation (from glass)
o
Rare mercury aspiration (if vomiting or poor swallowing)
Why the other options are incorrect:
Option Reason it's incorrect
A) Gastric lavage Contraindicated — risk of pushing glass fragments into tissues
B) Activated charcoal Ineffective — doesn’t bind metals like mercury
C) Dialysis
Used in severe inorganic/organic mercury poisoning, not elemental
ingestion
5) Succimer Chelator — used in organic/inorganic mercury, not needed here
6) Sodium calcium
edetate
Also a chelator for lead/inorganic mercury, not indicated here
Conclusion:
In accidental swallowing of mercury from a thermometer, elemental mercury is minimally absorbed,
and the appropriate management is observation only unless there are complications from broken glass.

stem: Patient treated with methotrexate and Abatacept. Which molecules involved in T cell co stimulation?
explanation:
Background:
The patient is being treated with:
•
Methotrexate – a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD)
•
Abatacept – a selective T-cell co-stimulation modulator used in rheumatoid arthritis
How Abatacept works:
•
Abatacept is a CTLA-4–Ig fusion protein
•
It binds to B7 molecules (CD80/CD86) on antigen-presenting cells (APCs)
•
This blocks interaction with CD28 on T-cells
•
Result: Prevents the second signal needed for full T-cell activation
T-cell activation requires two signals:
1. Signal 1:
o
TCR (T-cell receptor) recognizes antigen presented on MHC class II (or I) on APC
2. Signal 2 (Co-stimulation):
o
CD28 on T cell binds to B7 (CD80/86) on APC
Abatacept blocks this CD28–B7 interaction
Why other options are incorrect:
Option Explanation
MH1 class
Presents antigens to CD8+ T cells, involved in cytotoxic responses, not co-
stimulation
MH2 class Presents antigens to CD4+ T cells, part of signal 1, not co-stimulation
Toll-like
receptors
Part of innate immunity, not directly involved in T-cell co-stimulation
CD28 (B7) Correct – central to signal 2, the co-stimulatory signal blocked by Abatacept
Conclusion:
The key molecules involved in T-cell co-stimulation, and targeted by Abatacept, are CD28 on T cells
and B7 (CD80/86) on antigen-presenting cells.

stem: A 45 female presented with pain in Lt heel suddenly on walking. Known case HTN. Current medications include Amlodipine and Lisinopril. Regular co-codamol and ibuprofen for arthralgia Course of ciprofloxacin for E. coli pyelonephritis. What's the most likely cause of ruptured left Achilles tendon?
explanation:
Key clinical details:
•
45-year-old woman
•
Sudden onset heel pain while walking → strongly suggests Achilles tendon rupture
•
Medication history includes:
o Ciprofloxacin (recent course for UTI)
o
Amlodipine + Lisinopril (HTN)
o
Co-codamol + Ibuprofen (pain relief)
Ciprofloxacin and Tendon Rupture:
•
Fluoroquinolones (especially ciprofloxacin) are well-known to cause:
o
Tendinopathy
o
Achilles tendon rupture (most common site)
•
Risk factors include:
o
Age >60
o
Concurrent steroid use
o
Female sex
o Renal impairment
Although she’s 45 and not on steroids, ciprofloxacin alone can still cause tendon rupture, especially if
physically active.
Why other options are incorrect:
Drug Reason
Amlodipine Calcium channel blocker – not linked to tendon damage
Lisinopril ACE inhibitor – not associated with tendon rupture
Co-codamol Analgesic (paracetamol + codeine) – no effect on tendons
Ibuprofen NSAID – treats pain/inflammation, not linked to rupture
Conclusion:
The Achilles tendon rupture in this patient is most likely ciprofloxacin-induced tendinopathy, a
recognized adverse effect of fluoroquinolone antibiotics.

stem: A 6 weeks pregnant female, having history of 20 pack years smoking. Most appropriate therapy to quit smoking?
explanation:
Key considerations in pregnancy:
•
First-line approach for smoking cessation in pregnancy is always non-pharmacological.
•
Behavioral interventions like CBT and counseling are the safest and first-line therapies.
• Smoking in pregnancy is associated with:
o
Low birth weight
o
Miscarriage
o Preterm birth
Stillbirth
Why CBT is the most appropriate:
•
Safest method — no drug exposure to fetus
•
Shown to be effective, especially when combined with regular follow-up
•
Recommended first-line in most international guidelines (e.g., NICE, ACOG)
Why not the other options (especially in early pregnancy):
Option Why it's not appropriate in early pregnancy
1. Bupropion Not first-line; limited data in pregnancy; potential teratogenicity concern
2. Electronic cigarettes
Not recommended — unknown long-term fetal effects and may still
deliver nicotine
3. Varenicline Contraindicated in pregnancy due to lack of safety data
4. Nicotine Replacement
Therapy (NRT)
May be considered if behavioral support fails, but used with caution
due to nicotine's effect on fetal development
Conclusion:
In a 6-week pregnant woman, the most appropriate first-line therapy to quit smoking is Cognitive
Behavioural Therapy (CBT) — safest and guideline-recommended approach.

stem: Tolvaptan acts on?
explanation:
Mechanism of Action of Tolvaptan:
•
Tolvaptan is a selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist.
• It blocks the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) at the V2 receptors in the renal collecting
ducts.
•
This results in:
o Free water excretion (aquaresis)
o
Increased serum sodium levels without significant sodium loss
Clinical uses of Tolvaptan:
•
Hyponatremia due to SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion)
•
Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) — slows cyst growth and renal
decline
Why the others are incorrect:
Option Reason it's incorrect
GLP
Refers to glucagon-like peptide (incretin system); target for drugs like liraglutide, not
tolvaptan
SGLT2 Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 — target of drugs like dapagliflozin, not tolvaptan
Ca
Refers to calcium channel blockers — unrelated to tolvaptan’s mechanism
Conclusion:
Tolvaptan works by blocking the vasopressin V2 receptor, promoting free water excretion, and is used
in conditions like SIADH and ADPKD.

stem: 25 years old Female with HIV CD4+ 350 Which vaccine can lead to clinical disease?
explanation:
Key facts:
• Patient: 25-year-old female with HIV
•
CD4 count = 350 cells/mm³
•
Important threshold:
o
CD4 < 200 → high risk for opportunistic infections
o
CD4 < 500 → increased caution with live vaccines
Vaccines and HIV – which can cause clinical disease?
Vaccine Type Risk in HIV?
BCG
Live
attenuated
Contraindicated — can cause disseminated TB in HIV
Pneumococcal Inactivated Safe and recommended
Rubella Live attenuated
Generally avoided if CD4 < 200, but may be considered if >200–
500 depending on setting
Hep B Inactivated Safe and recommended
Tetanus
Inactivated
toxoid
Safe and recommended
Measles
Live
attenuated
Risky if CD4 < 200, but may be used if CD4 > 200–500, depending
on local guidelines
Why BCG is the correct answer:
•
Live attenuated vaccine
• Should not be given to HIV-positive individuals due to risk of:
o
Disseminated BCG infection
o
Especially dangerous even with CD4 > 200
Conclusion:
Among the options, BCG is the only live vaccine that can definitely cause clinical disease in an HIV-
positive patient, even at CD4 count of 350.

stem: A 45 year pt with schizoaffective was unable to get out of his bed, slightly confused. Current medications include fluoxetine. Has been started on IV injection for his mental health but the pt did not remember the name. O/E: Tachycardic and tachypneic High temperature of 39 and hypertensive with increase rigidity. Dx?
explanation:
Key clinical features:
•
45-year-old with schizoaffective disorder
•
Started on an unknown injection for mental health → likely a depot antipsychotic
•
On fluoxetine (an SSRI)
•
Now presents with:
o
Confusion
o Inability to get out of bed
o
Tachycardia, tachypnoea
o
Fever (39°C)
o
Hypertension
o
Marked rigidity
Why Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome is correct:
•
Classic features of NMS:
o
Hyperthermia
o
Muscle rigidity ("lead pipe")
o
Autonomic instability (e.g., tachycardia, hypertension)
o
Altered mental status
•
Triggered by dopamine blockade (i.e., antipsychotics, particularly typical or depot forms)
•
Usually occurs within days to weeks of starting or increasing the dose
Why not the others:
Option Reason it's less likely
1. Acute
Parkinsonism
Can cause rigidity, but no hyperthermia, autonomic instability, or confusion to
this degree
2. Amphetamine
toxicity
Causes agitation, hyperthermia, but typically no rigidity and more CNS
excitation
3. Serotonin
Syndrome
Can look similar, but usually causes clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, not lead-pipe
rigidity; also associated with diarrhea and mydriasis
Conclusion:
This patient has the classic triad of hyperthermia, rigidity, and altered mental status with recent
antipsychotic exposure, making Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) the most likely diagnosis.

stem: In bullous pemphigoid which one is true?
options: Linear IgG deposition in basement membrane
Linear IgA deposition in basement membrane
explanation:
Bullous Pemphigoid: Key Facts:
•
Autoimmune blistering skin disease seen typically in the elderly.
Caused by autoantibodies (IgG) directed against hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and
BP230) in the basement membrane zone.
•
This leads to separation of the epidermis from the dermis, causing subepidermal blisters.
Immunopathology:
•
Direct immunofluorescence shows:
o Linear deposition of IgG (± C3) along the basement membrane zone
Why the other options are incorrect:
Option Why it's incorrect
Intracellular IgG deposition in epidermis Seen in Pemphigus vulgaris, not bullous pemphigoid
IgA deposition in basement membrane Suggests linear IgA disease, not bullous pemphigoid
Linear IgA deposition in basement membrane Seen in Linear IgA bullous dermatosis, not BP
Conclusion:
In bullous pemphigoid, the hallmark finding is linear IgG deposition along the basement membrane,
making that the correct answer.

stem: 70 yr old male with pancreatic cancer, increased pain on diamorphine 240 mg in 24 hrs What dose of diamorphine should be given for break through pain?
explanation:
Key principle: Managing breakthrough pain in opioid use
•
For patients on regular opioid infusions (e.g., diamorphine), the breakthrough (rescue) dose is
typically calculated as:
1/6th of the total 24-hour opioid dose
In this case:
•
Total 24-hour diamorphine dose = 240 mg
• 1/6 of 240 mg = 40 mg
Therefore, the correct breakthrough dose = 40 mg
This would be administered as needed for episodes of breakthrough pain, in addition to the regular
continuous infusion.
Conclusion:
For a patient on diamorphine 240 mg over 24 hours, the correct breakthrough dose is 40 mg, which is
1/6th of the total daily dose.

stem: 68 year old male with vascular problem, acute bloody diarrhoea, HTN. CT - Ischemic colitis. Which part of colon is most commonly affected?
explanation:
Key clinical scenario:
•
68-year-old male
• Hypertension + vascular disease → risk factors for mesenteric hypoperfusion
•
Acute bloody diarrhoea
•
CT: Ischemic colitis
Most commonly affected site in ischemic colitis:
Splenic flexure — a classic watershed area, where:
•
SMA (superior mesenteric artery) and IMA (inferior mesenteric artery) territories overlap
•
Vulnerable to hypoperfusion and ischemia during systemic hypotension or vascular compromise
Other commonly affected watershed areas:
•
Rectosigmoid junction — between IMA and internal iliac artery
•
But splenic flexure is most classically involved
Conclusion:
In ischemic colitis, especially in elderly patients with vascular risk, the splenic flexure is the most
common site affected due to its watershed blood supply.

stem: 45 year old female suddenly developed acute left hemiplegia. She was diagnosed with SAH 6 days ago, and treated with surgery. The recovery was uneventful. What is the cause of this new onset deficit?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
•
45-year-old female with sudden onset left hemiplegia
•
Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) diagnosed 6 days ago
• Treated surgically, initial recovery was uneventful
•
Now develops a new focal neurological deficit
Why the answer is Cerebral Vasospasm:
•
Cerebral vasospasm is a well-known complication of SAH, particularly:
o
Occurs typically 3–14 days after SAH (most commonly days 5–9)
o Caused by arterial narrowing in response to blood breakdown products in the
subarachnoid space
o
Leads to delayed cerebral ischemia, presenting as focal neurological deficits like
hemiplegia
Why not the others:
Option Why it’s incorrect
B. Recurrent
SAH
Unlikely after definitive surgical treatment and uneventful recovery; would present with
sudden severe headache, reduced consciousness, not focal hemiplegia alone
C.
Hyponatremia
Common post-SAH (e.g., from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting), but usually causes
confusion, seizures, not isolated hemiplegia
D. Stroke
and vasospasm is the underlying cause here — so vasospasm is the best answer
Conclusion:
In a patient developing a new focal neurological deficit several days after SAH, the most likely cause is
cerebral vasospasm, a common and potentially reversible complication occurring around day 5–9 post-
SAH.

stem: 60 year old with mixed overdose of fluoxetine and Zuclopenthixol Hyper reflexia clonus 39.2 Dx?
explanation:
Key clinical features in this scenario:
•
60-year-old with mixed overdose:
o
Fluoxetine → SSRI → increases serotonin
o Zuclopenthixol → typical antipsychotic → can cause NMS, but not serotonergic
•
Clinical signs:
o
Hyperreflexia
o Clonus
o
High fever (39.2°C)
Serotonin Syndrome vs Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS):
Feature Serotonin Syndrome NMS
Onset Rapid (within hours) Slower (1–3 days)
Neuromuscular Hyperreflexia, clonus, tremor Lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia
Mental state Agitation, confusion Confusion, stupor
Temperature ↑↑↑ (can be high in both) ↑↑↑
Pupils Often dilated Normal
Cause
Serotonergic drugs (e.g. SSRI, MAOI, SNRI,
MDMA)
Dopamine antagonists (e.g.
antipsychotics)
Why Serotonin Syndrome is correct here:
•
Fluoxetine overdose is a strong serotonergic trigger
•
Hyperreflexia and clonus are hallmark signs of serotonin syndrome
•
Rapid onset and high fever support diagnosis
•
Zuclopenthixol may contribute, but the features are more in line with serotonin toxicity
Conclusion:
The presence of clonus, hyperreflexia, and high fever in a patient with fluoxetine overdose points
clearly to Serotonin Syndrome, not NMS.

stem: 2 months of weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, increased diabetes Despite increasing dose of metformin, Also has central obesity and mild hirsutism. Currently on Lisinopril, Amlodipine and atorvastatin. Most likely explanation?
explanation:
Key clinical features:
• 2 months of weight gain
•
Proximal muscle weakness
Worsening glycemic control (increased diabetes)
•
Medications: Lisinopril, Amlodipine, Atorvastatin
These findings are classic for Cushing syndrome, a condition of excess glucocorticoids, whether
endogenous (e.g. adrenal or pituitary tumors) or exogenous (steroids).
Why Cushing Syndrome is the most likely:
•
Proximal muscle weakness is due to catabolic effect of cortisol on muscles
•
Weight gain, particularly truncal and facial (though not mentioned, suggested by rapid gain)
• Worsening diabetes is very common due to insulin resistance
•
Onset over weeks to months is typical for Cushing syndrome
Why not the other options:
Option Why it's less likely
Statin-induced
myopathy
Can cause muscle pain/weakness, but does not cause weight gain or worsen
diabetes; also usually causes myalgia, not isolated proximal weakness
Diabetic
amyotrophy
Typically causes painful asymmetric proximal leg weakness, weight loss, and
occurs in long-standing diabetes, not early or worsening diabetes with weight
gain
Conclusion:
The combination of weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, and deteriorating diabetes suggests
Cushing syndrome as the most likely diagnosis.

stem: 25 yr old woman with Crohn's disease on long-term parenteral nutrition presents with progressive dyspnoea. Echo shows dilated cardiomyopathy. Which micronutrient deficiency is responsible?
explanation:
Key concept: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and nutritional deficiency
•
Among trace elements, selenium deficiency is a well-established cause of dilated
cardiomyopathy.
• It leads to a condition called Keshan disease, historically described in selenium-deficient regions
of China.
Mechanism:
•
Selenium is essential for the activity of glutathione peroxidase, an enzyme that protects cardiac
myocytes from oxidative damage.
•
Deficiency can lead to:
o Myocardial cell injury
o
Progressive left ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction
o
Ultimately heart failure
Manganese:
•
Manganese is required for some enzymatic functions but is not associated with
cardiomyopathy.
•
Deficiency is rare and does not cause heart failure or DCM.
Conclusion:
In a case of dilated cardiomyopathy or heart failure, selenium deficiency is the relevant nutritional
etiology, not manganese
A young girl came from right sided weakness. His father moved out for 1 years (divorce). She loved her
father most. She came to GP for right hand and right leg weakness but examination found all are normal
Dx?
A. Conversion disorder
B. Somatic symptom disorder
C. Hypochondrial disorder
D. Adjustment disorder
E. Dysthymia
ANSWERS:
Conversion disorder
Correct answer: A. Conversion disorder
Key features from the scenario:
•
Young girl with sudden right-sided weakness
•
Neurological symptoms (right hand and leg weakness) reported
• No neurological abnormality on examination (normal power, tone, reflexes)
•
Emotional stressor: father left a year ago — strong emotional bond disrupted
•
Presents to GP — suggests functional symptoms, not malingering
Why Conversion Disorder is correct:
•
Conversion disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) involves:
o
Neurological symptoms (e.g., weakness, paralysis, non-epileptic seizures)
o
Not explained by medical disease
o
Often triggered by psychological stress or trauma
o
Patient is not faking the symptoms; symptoms are real to them
Why other options are incorrect:
Option Why it’s incorrect
B. Somatic symptom disorder
Involves chronic physical complaints with excessive worry;
typically not neurological deficits
C. Hypochondriasis (now Illness
Anxiety Disorder)
Characterized by preoccupation with having a serious illness,
not neurological loss of function
D. Adjustment disorder
Emotional or behavioral symptoms following stressor, but not
neurological symptoms
E. Dysthymia
Chronic mild depression, not associated with sudden
neurological symptoms
Conclusion:
This presentation of sudden weakness without physical findings, following an emotional stressor, is
classic for Conversion Disorder — a subtype of somatic symptom and related disorders involving
functional neurological symptoms.

stem: Splenectomy done 4 years back Most common finding?
explanation:
Key concept: Post-splenectomy peripheral blood findings
After splenectomy (or in cases of functional asplenia), the spleen’s filtering function is lost, leading to
the persistence of certain red blood cell inclusions in the circulation that would otherwise be removed
by the spleen.
Howell–Jolly bodies:
•
DNA remnants in red blood cells
•
Normally cleared by the spleen
•
Seen in:
o
Post-splenectomy
o
Functional asplenia (e.g., sickle cell disease)
•
Most common and classic finding after splenectomy
Why the others are incorrect:
