Inclusion Description Relevance
Pappenheimer
bodies
Iron-containing
granules
Can be seen post-splenectomy, but less common than
Howell–Jolly bodies
Heinz bodies
Denatured
hemoglobin
Seen in G6PD deficiency or unstable hemoglobin disorders;
not typical after splenectomy
Conclusion:
The most common peripheral blood smear finding in a patient who had a splenectomy is the
presence of Howell–Jolly bodies.

stem: An ankylosing spondylitis pt on diclofenac sodium for 4 weeks, DAS28 score high The patient had tried two different NSAIDs for 4 weeks. Next line of management?
explanation:
Key facts: Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) management
•
First-line treatment: NSAIDs
o
Used to control pain and stiffness
o
Trial of at least 2 different NSAIDs over several weeks is recommended before escalation
•
Disease Activity Assessment:
o DAS28 is more commonly used for rheumatoid arthritis, but if mentioned here, it's
suggesting high disease activity
o
In AS, we typically use BASDAI or ASDAS, but high disease activity despite NSAIDs
warrants biologics
Why Adalimumab is correct:
• Adalimumab is a TNF-alpha inhibitor (biologic)
•
Indicated in axial spondyloarthritis/AS with persistent high disease activity despite NSAIDs
•
Approved and highly effective for reducing symptoms, inflammation, and improving function
Why other options are incorrect:
Option Why it’s incorrect
Anakinra IL-1 inhibitor — not effective in AS, used in autoinflammatory syndromes or RA
Methotrexate
(MTX)
Has limited efficacy in axial disease; more helpful in peripheral arthritis (e.g., in
PsA or RA)
Rituximab Targets B cells (CD20) — used in RA, not effective in AS
Sulfasalazine
May help in peripheral joint involvement in AS, but not useful in axial disease,
and not first choice after failed NSAIDs
Conclusion:
For a patient with ankylosing spondylitis, high disease activity, and failure of two NSAIDs, the
appropriate next step is initiation of a TNF inhibitor, such as Adalimumab.

stem: 30 yrs with recurrent rectal bleeding. Father and grandfather has > 10 rectal polys and later carcinoma. Investigations show Px has > 100 polys and R211 panel was done and show heterozygous…… (I can’t remember the full finding ) What is the most common finding?
explanation:
Key clinical features:
• 30-year-old with recurrent rectal bleeding
•
Strong family history: father and grandfather had >10 polyps and later colorectal cancer
•
Patient has >100 polyps on investigation
•
Genetic testing (e.g., R211 panel) done — likely revealing APC mutation
•
All these point toward a diagnosis of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)
Why APC gene mutation is correct:
•
FAP is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the APC (Adenomatous
Polyposis Coli) gene
• Characterized by:
o
Development of hundreds to thousands of adenomatous colorectal polyps
o
Near 100% risk of colorectal cancer by middle age if untreated
•
Genetic testing often reveals heterozygous APC gene mutation
Why not the other options:
Option Why it’s incorrect
A.
Adenomatous
Describes the histological type of the polyps (true in FAP), but not the genetic cause
— APC mutation is the best, most specific answer
B.
Inflammatory
Seen in inflammatory bowel disease — unrelated to polyposis syndromes
C. Hyperplastic Associated with non-neoplastic polyps; not typically precancerous or inherited
D. Serrated
Seen in Serrated Polyposis Syndrome, which has a different genetic background and
presentation (usually fewer polyps than FAP)
Conclusion:
In a young patient with >100 colorectal polyps and a strong family history of polyposis and cancer,
the most likely and specific finding is an APC gene mutation, confirming Familial Adenomatous
Polyposis (FAP).

stem: A 25 year old woman presents with anaemia (no symptoms, no abdominal signs). Investigations are normal except mild anaemia. She is menstruating regularly. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Key scenario points:
• 25-year-old woman
•
Mild microcytic anemia:
o
Hb = 10 g/dL
o
MCV = 78 fL
•
Ferritin = 10 → iron deficiency
• Anti-TTG <15 → negative for coeliac disease
•
No GI symptoms (no pain, tenderness, or bleeding)
Physically well
Why "No further investigation" is correct:
•
In young, premenopausal women, the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia (IDA)
is:
Menstrual blood loss
• If the patient is:
o
Asymptomatic
o
Without red flags (weight loss, GI bleeding, family history of colon cancer, etc.)
o Negative coeliac screen
→ Then empirical iron replacement therapy is appropriate without further GI
investigations
Why not endoscopy or colonoscopy:
Test Reason it's not needed
Endoscopy
Used to rule out upper GI causes (e.g., coeliac, ulcers) — but coeliac screen is negative
and no upper GI symptoms
Colonoscopy
Used to rule out lower GI blood loss (e.g., colon cancer, IBD) — no red flags, age is low,
and she’s asymptomatic
Conclusion:
In a young, asymptomatic premenopausal woman with iron deficiency anemia and no red flag
features, the appropriate next step is no further investigation — start oral iron therapy and monitor
response.

stem: 70 year old COPD patient with breathlessness, decreased breath sounds, polycythaemia, oedema. Criteria for long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT)?
explanation:
Key scenario features:
•
70-year-old with COPD
• Breathlessness, decreased breath sounds
•
Signs of chronic hypoxia:
o
Polycythaemia (increased red cell mass to compensate for low O₂)
o Oedema (suggests cor pulmonale or right heart strain)
These are classic indicators to consider Long-Term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT).
LTOT Criteria (per BTS/NICE guidelines):
LTOT is indicated when arterial blood gases (on room air at rest and stable clinical state) show:
1. PaO₂ ≤ 7.3 kPa
This is the primary threshold
2. PaO₂ ≤ 8.0 kPa plus one or more of:
•
Secondary polycythaemia
•
Peripheral oedema
•
Pulmonary hypertension
In this case:
• PaO₂ < 7.7 (i.e., under 8.0)
•
Patient has polycythaemia + oedema
Meets criteria for LTOT
Why other options are incorrect:
Option Why it's incorrect
SpO₂ < 92% Not sufficient alone — must confirm with arterial blood gas (PaO₂)
PaO₂ < 8.2 Slightly above standard cut-off — does not independently meet criteria
Alveolar
gradient >2
Not relevant to LTOT decision-making; used in assessing gas exchange efficiency,
not oxygen therapy indication
Conclusion:
This COPD patient with PaO₂ < 7.7 kPa, polycythaemia, and oedema meets the criteria for LTOT,
making PaO₂ < 7.7 the correct answer.

stem: Young male came up with hemoptysis X Ray - upper lobe collapse What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
•
Young male
Presents with hemoptysis
•
Chest X-ray: shows upper lobe collapse
Why Bronchial Carcinoma is the most likely diagnosis:
•
While bronchial carcinoma is more common in older individuals, certain types like
bronchoalveolar carcinoma (now under adenocarcinoma spectrum) or smoking-related
squamous cell carcinoma can affect younger patients, especially smokers.
•
Lobar collapse (especially upper lobe) with hemoptysis strongly suggests a central obstructing
mass, which is classic for bronchial carcinoma.
• Collapse occurs due to tumor obstructing a major bronchus, leading to resorption atelectasis.
Why not the others:
Diagnosis Why it’s less likely
Bronchial
carcinoid
Can cause hemoptysis, but rare, and typically causes recurrent infections or
episodic bleeding without lobe collapse
Bronchiectasis
Causes hemoptysis and recurrent infections, but typically shows tram-track or ring
shadows, not lobar collapse on imaging
Conclusion:
In a young male with hemoptysis and upper lobe collapse on CXR, the most likely diagnosis is
bronchial carcinoma, as it most commonly causes lobar collapse via bronchial obstruction.

stem: Young female with paracetamol overdose (24 tablets) 9 hours ago, asymptomatic with suicidal intent. Most appropriate management?
explanation:
Key scenario features:
•
Young female, intentional overdose
•
Paracetamol 500 mg × 24 tablets = 12 grams
• Weight = 60 kg
•
Presentation 9 hours post-ingestion
•
Asymptomatic, but suicidal intent is present
Toxicity threshold:
•
Toxic paracetamol dose:
o 150 mg/kg = potentially hepatotoxic
o
For 60 kg → 150 × 60 = 9 grams
o
She took 12 grams → toxic dose
•
Presentation is after 8 hours, so activated charcoal is no longer effective.
Why N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is correct:
• NAC is the antidote for paracetamol overdose
•
Most effective within 8 hours, but still indicated up to 24 hours, especially if dose is toxic
•
Should be started immediately while awaiting paracetamol level if >8 hours post-ingestion
Why other options are incorrect:
Option Why it's not appropriate
Gastric lavage Only useful within 1 hour of ingestion; otherwise harmful
Psychiatric review Important, but only after medical stabilization
Activated charcoal Effective within 1 hour; not helpful at 9 hours
Conclusion:
In a patient presenting 9 hours after a toxic paracetamol overdose, the immediate and most
appropriate step is to start N-acetylcysteine, even if asymptomatic. Psychiatric review should follow
after medical stabilization.

stem: Man with severe edema (50+ age) Low serum albumin Urine protein:creatinine ratio around 400 Renal biopsy - normal on microscopy and immunofluorescence Dx?
explanation:
Key features:
•
Older man (>50)
•
Severe oedema
•
Low serum albumin
•
Urine protein:creatinine ratio ~400 → nephrotic-range proteinuria
• Renal biopsy: normal light microscopy and normal immunofluorescence
Why Minimal Change Disease (MCD) is correct:
•
MCD is classically associated with:
o
Nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, oedema)
o
Normal light microscopy
o
Negative immunofluorescence
o
Diagnosis confirmed by electron microscopy showing podocyte foot process
effacement
• Though more common in children, MCD can occur in adults, including those over 50
Why not the other options:
Option Why it's incorrect
Membranous
Glomerulonephritis (MGN)
Would show thickened capillary walls on LM and granular IgG/C3
deposition on IF
Multiple Myeloma (MM)
Would typically show cast nephropathy, light chain deposition, and
may show abnormalities on IF or LM; also associated with hypercalcemia,
anemia, and bone lesions
Renal vein thrombosis
Can be a complication of nephrotic syndrome but not the primary
cause; doesn’t explain normal biopsy findings on LM and IF
In a patient with nephrotic syndrome and normal renal biopsy on LM and IF, the most likely diagnosis
is Minimal Change Disease (MCD) — even in older adults.

stem: A 16 yr female + dehydration, confusion, Abd pain, vomiting RBS 17 Metabolic acidosis Insulin infusion given Next step in management?
explanation:
Key scenario features:
•
16-year-old female with:
o
Dehydration
o
Confusion, abdominal pain, vomiting
o
Random blood sugar = 17 mmol/L
o Metabolic acidosis
o
Treated with insulin infusion
This is Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) — a medical emergency.
Why IV Normal Saline is the next step:
• First priority in DKA is fluid resuscitation to:
o
Restore circulating volume
Improve renal perfusion
o
Support tissue perfusion
o
Reduce counterregulatory hormone levels
• 0.9% Normal Saline (NS) is the fluid of choice initially
•
Insulin should already be started, but rehydration is critical
Why not the other options:
Option Why it’s incorrect
IV Colloid Not indicated — crystalloids (NS) are first-line; colloids are not routinely used in DKA
IV Sodium
Bicarbonate
Only used in severe acidosis (pH < 6.9) and life-threatening cases; routine use is
discouraged due to risks (e.g., hypokalemia, paradoxical CNS acidosis)
LMWH
Prophylactic anticoagulation may be considered in older or immobile patients, but
not an immediate priority in a 16-year-old unless other risk factors are present
Conclusion:
In a young patient with DKA already on insulin, the immediate next step is IV normal saline, to correct
dehydration and hypovolemia, which is central to early DKA management.

stem: A Female presented with abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea, she was previously investigated for primary infertility, she has used ibuprofen for arthritis, later on stopped ibuprofen and used omeprazole for 4weeks but still there is no resolution of symptoms On EGD - multiple duodenal ulcers Rapid urease H. pylori - negative Hb 128 Calcium 2.8 (elevated value) Po4 - near normal value Alb normal Dx?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
•
Female with abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea
•
Multiple duodenal ulcers on EGD
•
Rapid urease test (for H. pylori) = negative
•
History of primary infertility
•
Ibuprofen stopped but no improvement
•
Elevated serum calcium = 2.8 mmol/L
• Normal phosphate and albumin
Interpretation:
Multiple duodenal ulcers + watery diarrhoea
•
Strongly suggestive of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (ZES) due to gastrinoma — a gastrin-
secreting tumor causing massive acid production
Hypercalcemia with normal phosphate
•
Suggests primary hyperparathyroidism (not secondary causes like renal failure)
Primary infertility
•
May be linked to pituitary dysfunction (e.g., prolactinoma)
These three features — gastrinoma, primary hyperparathyroidism, and possibly a pituitary tumor —
are the classical triad of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1).
Why MEN 1 is correct
MEN 1 typically involves the "3 Ps":
1. Parathyroid hyperplasia/adenoma → hypercalcemia
2. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors → gastrinoma (ZES) → multiple duodenal ulcers +
diarrhoea
3. Pituitary tumors → may present with infertility, galactorrhoea, amenorrhea
Why other options are less likely:
Option Why it's incorrect
4. Cushing’s
Causes hyperglycemia, hypertension, hypokalemia — not multiple ulcers or
hypercalcemia
5. Crohn’s
Can cause diarrhoea and pain but does not cause hypercalcemia or multiple
duodenal ulcers
6. Small intestine
lymphoma
May cause diarrhoea and pain, but not hypercalcemia or gastric acid
overproduction
7. Ibuprofen-
induced gastritis
NSAIDs can cause ulcers but not multiple duodenal ulcers, not diarrhoea, and
not hypercalcemia — and stopping ibuprofen didn’t help
Conclusion:
The combination of multiple duodenal ulcers, watery diarrhoea, and hypercalcemia in a patient with a
history of infertility points strongly toward MEN 1, with a likely gastrinoma and parathyroid adenoma
as components.

stem: Patient presents with bilirubin 81, S ALT- 72, Alk phosphate - 532 GGT- 650 Has been taking levofloxacin, Co-amoxiclav for 2 months. What is the cause of this picture?
explanation:
Key interpretation of LFTs:
•
Bilirubin: 81 µmol/L – elevated
•
ALT: 72 U/L – mildly elevated
• ALP: 532 U/L – markedly elevated
•
GGT: 650 U/L – markedly elevated
This is a cholestatic pattern of liver injury:
•
ALP and GGT disproportionately elevated relative to ALT
•
Suggests biliary tract involvement or drug-induced cholestasis
Causative agent:
Co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin-clavulanate)
•
Well-known cause of cholestatic or mixed-pattern drug-induced liver injury (DILI)
•
Reaction may occur:
o
During or after prolonged use
o
Idiosyncratically — not dose-dependent
• Typically seen in older adults or prolonged use
Levofloxacin
•
Can cause liver injury, but:
o
Usually hepatocellular rather than cholestatic
o
Much less commonly associated with significant liver enzyme elevation
Conclusion:
The marked cholestatic liver enzyme elevation with jaundice in a patient who has been on Co-
amoxiclav for 2 months is most consistent with Co-amoxiclav-induced cholestatic liver injury.

stem: 62 year old man with terminal RCC, on morphine sulphate. Develops increased drowsiness. Creatinine is elevated. Which metabolite is responsible?
explanation:
Key points:
•
62-year-old man with terminal renal cell carcinoma
•
On morphine sulphate
• Now with increased drowsiness
•
Bloods show:
o
↑ Creatinine → renal impairment
o ↑ Bilirubin, ↑ ALT → hepatic impairment as well
Pharmacology of Morphine:
• Morphine is metabolized in the liver to:
1. Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G) – active metabolite, potent analgesic, and sedative
2. Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) – inactive but can cause neurotoxic effects
•
These metabolites are renally excreted.
In renal impairment, especially in terminal patients:
•
M6G accumulates → crosses the blood–brain barrier
•
Leads to:
o Sedation
o
Drowsiness
o
In some cases, respiratory depression
Conclusion:
The metabolite that accumulates in renal impairment, causing increased drowsiness in this patient on
morphine, is 6-morphine-glucuronide (M6G).

stem: A 19 year old female with 3-day rash on legs and bruises on trunk. Hb 119, WBC 5.2, Platelets 9. No lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
•
19-year-old female
•
3-day history of rash on legs (likely petechiae/purpura)
•
Bruises on trunk and limbs → spontaneous bleeding
•
Investigations:
o Platelets = 2 × 10⁹/L (very low)
o
Hb = 119 g/L (normal)
o
WBC = 5.2 × 10⁹/L (normal)
o Blood film: platelets absent, no abnormal cells
Why Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP) is correct:
•
ITP is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies destroy platelets.
•
Often occurs in young females
•
Presents with:
o Petechiae, purpura
o
Mucosal bleeding or bruising
•
Lab findings:
o
Isolated thrombocytopenia
o
Normal Hb and WBC
o
Normal blood film apart from low platelets
Why the other options are incorrect:
Option Why it’s less likely
A) HIV
Can cause thrombocytopenia, but would usually present with other systemic features; not the
most likely initial presentation
B) DIC
Would show low platelets + prolonged PT/aPTT, schistocytes on blood film, and abnormal
coagulation profile
3) TTP
Would show microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA): anemia, schistocytes,
neurological signs, renal dysfunction — none present here
1. ALL
like fatigue, infection, etc. — not isolated thrombocytopenia
Conclusion:
This is a classic presentation of Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP) — a young woman with isolated
severe thrombocytopenia, normal Hb and WBC, and a normal film except absent platelets.

stem: A female presents with one dilated pupil, poor reaction to light but preserved near response (accommodation). What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Key clinical features of Holmes-Adie Pupil:
•
Typically affects young females
•
One pupil is tonically dilated (larger than the other)
•
Reacts poorly to light, but better to accommodation (light-near dissociation)
•
Usually unilateral
•
Often associated with loss of deep tendon reflexes (in some cases)
Diagnosis clues in your case:
•
Female
•
One dilated pupil
Poor response to both light and accommodation
o
In Holmes-Adie pupil, the accommodation response is usually better than light
response, but both may be sluggish
• Suggests tonic pupil = Holmes-Adie
Conclusion:
A tonically dilated pupil with poor light and accommodation reaction, especially if unilateral and in a
young woman, is characteristic of a Holmes-Adie pupil.

stem: Muscle responsible for ankle clonus?
explanation:
Ankle clonus – key concept:
•
Clonus is a series of involuntary, rhythmic, muscular contractions and relaxations.
• At the ankle, clonus is tested by sudden dorsiflexion of the foot.
•
This stretches the gastrocnemius–soleus complex (part of the triceps surae group), triggering
rhythmic contraction via hyperactive stretch reflexes.
Gastrocnemius:
•
A calf muscle that:
o Plantarflexes the ankle
o
Is stretched during forced dorsiflexion
Contracts reflexively in clonus
•
It is the primary muscle involved in ankle clonus
Other muscles:
Muscle Role
Tibialis Posterior Inverts the foot and assists plantarflexion, but not the main driver of clonus
Flexor Hallucis Longus Flexes the big toe; assists plantarflexion but not the primary muscle in clonus
Conclusion:
The gastrocnemius is the main muscle responsible for ankle clonus, as it is the key plantarflexor
involved in the rhythmic contractions seen during the reflex.

stem: A 22 years old man presents with increase pedal edema and periorbital swelling. Urinalysis shows protein 4+ What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Key clinical features:
•
22-year-old male
• Presents with:
o
Pedal edema
o
Periorbital swelling
→ Classic signs of nephrotic syndrome
•
Urinalysis: Protein 4+ → nephrotic-range proteinuria
o This typically corresponds to >3.5 g/day
Why Minimal Change Disease (MCD) is most likely:
•
Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, but also occurs in young adults
•
Presents with:
o
Sudden-onset edema
o
Massive proteinuria
o
Normal or near-normal renal function
•
Urine is bland (no hematuria or casts)
• Renal biopsy is normal on light microscopy but shows podocyte foot process effacement on
electron microscopy
Why not the others:
Diagnosis Why it's less likely
Membranous Nephropathy
More common in middle-aged adults and associated with
autoimmune disease, malignancy, or hepatitis; often seen in men
40
Focal Segmental
Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
More common in African descent, associated with hypertension,
obesity, or HIV; often shows hematuria and hypertension in addition
to proteinuria
Conclusion:
In a young adult with heavy proteinuria and edema, the most likely diagnosis is Minimal Change
Nephropathy, especially in the absence of hematuria or hypertension.
Rheumatoid arthritis + Restrictive picture on PFTs
Dx?
Asthma
Emphysema
Bronchiolitis obliterans
Pulmonary fibrosis
Rheumatoid nodules
ANSWERS:
Pulmonary fibrosis
Correct answer: Pulmonary fibrosis
Key reasoning:
• Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic inflammatory disease that can affect the lungs.
•
The most common pulmonary manifestation of RA that leads to a restrictive pattern on
pulmonary function tests (PFTs) is interstitial lung disease (ILD), specifically pulmonary
fibrosis.
Restrictive pattern on PFTs:
• ↓ Total Lung Capacity (TLC)
•
↓ Forced Vital Capacity (FVC)
•
Normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio
This pattern is typical of interstitial (fibrotic) lung disease, not obstructive diseases
Pulmonary fibrosis in RA:
• Common extra-articular manifestation
•
Causes:
o
Progressive dyspnea
o
Dry cough
o
Bibasal crackles on auscultation
• Confirmed by HRCT chest and restrictive PFT pattern
Why other options are incorrect:
Diagnosis Reason
Asthma Obstructive disease; causes reduced FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio — not restrictive
Emphysema Obstructive pattern; decreased diffusion capacity, but not restrictive
Bronchiolitis
obliterans
Rare in RA, causes obstructive or mixed pattern, not classic restrictive picture
Rheumatoid
nodules
Can be present in lungs but do not cause a restrictive PFT pattern unless
extensive — fibrosis is a more direct and common cause of restriction
Conclusion:
In a patient with RA and restrictive lung function, the most likely diagnosis is pulmonary fibrosis due
to interstitial lung disease, a known and serious pulmonary complication of RA.

stem: Age related macular degeneration Strongest risk factors?
explanation:
Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) – Key risk factors:
•
AMD is a leading cause of central vision loss in older adults.
•
It affects the macula, leading to gradual loss of sharp, central vision.
Strongest modifiable risk factor:
•
Smoking is the most well-established and strongest modifiable risk factor for both early and
late AMD.
o
It increases oxidative stress on the retina.
o
Associated with faster progression to neovascular (wet) AMD.
o
Smokers are 2–4 times more likely to develop AMD than non-smokers.
Other options:
Risk Factor Explanation
Diabetes Associated more with diabetic retinopathy, not AMD specifically
Long-term corticosteroids Can contribute to cataracts or glaucoma, but not strongly linked to AMD
Conclusion:
Among the listed options, smoking is the strongest and most direct risk factor for age-related
macular degeneration (AMD)
Nephritis after 24 hours of sore throat.
Dx?
IgA Nephropathy
ANSWERS:
IgA Nephropathy
Correct answer: IgA Nephropathy
Key clinical feature:
•
Nephritic syndrome (e.g., hematuria, proteinuria, ± hypertension, ± reduced GFR)
•
Occurring within 24–48 hours after a mucosal infection such as:
o Sore throat
o
Respiratory tract infection
o
Gastrointestinal infection
This pattern is typical of IgA Nephropathy (Berger's disease).
Why IgA Nephropathy is the diagnosis:
•
It is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide.
•
Caused by IgA immune complex deposition in the mesangium.
•
Classic presentation:
o
Hematuria (often macroscopic)
o
Starts within 24–48 hours of an upper respiratory tract infection or sore throat
o
May be recurrent
Why it's not post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis:
• PSGN occurs 1–3 weeks after streptococcal infection (throat or skin)
•
Typically shows low complement levels and a latent period, not immediate onset
Conclusion:
Nephritic features developing within 24 hours of a sore throat strongly suggest IgA Nephropathy, not
post-infectious GN.

stem: Which factor is the most important indicator of poor prognosis in malignant melanoma?
explanation:
Malignant Melanoma – Prognostic Factors
The most important and strongest prognostic factor in malignant melanoma is:
▪ Breslow thickness — the depth (in mm) of invasion from the granular layer of the epidermis to
the deepest point of tumor invasion.
Breslow Thickness – Prognostic Significance:
Thickness Prognosis
≤ 1.0 mm Excellent
1.01–2.0 mm Intermediate
2.01–4.0 mm Poorer
4.0 mm Worst prognosis
Other factors (less important than thickness but still relevant):
•
Ulceration – worsens prognosis
•
Lymph node involvement
•
Distant metastases
•
Mitotic rate – now used in staging thinner melanomas
•
Anatomic location (e.g., scalp/neck worse than limbs)
•
Patient age and sex
Common misconception:
•
Diameter or color changes are important for detection, but not key prognostic factors.
Conclusion:
The single most important prognostic factor in malignant melanoma is Breslow thickness — the
vertical depth of tumor invasion, which directly correlates with risk of metastasis and survival.

stem: Colonic Angiodysplasia, associated heart murmur?
explanation:
Key association:
•
Colonic angiodysplasia (especially in the cecum and right colon) is classically associated with:
o
Aortic stenosis is known as Heyde’s syndrome
Heyde’s Syndrome =
Aortic stenosis + Colonic angiodysplasia + Gastrointestinal bleeding
•
Thought to be due to:
o
Shear stress across a stenotic aortic valve → causes acquired von Willebrand factor
(vWF) deficiency
o
Leads to bleeding tendency, particularly from fragile colonic angiodysplastic vessels
Murmur in aortic stenosis:
• Ejection systolic murmur (also called crescendo–decrescendo murmur)
•
Heard best at the right upper sternal border
•
Often radiates to the carotids
Pansystolic murmur:
•
Typically heard in:
o Mitral regurgitation
o
Tricuspid regurgitation
o
Ventricular septal defect
•
Not associated with aortic stenosis or Heyde’s syndrome
Conclusion:
In a patient with colonic angiodysplasia, the associated murmur in Heyde’s syndrome is an ejection
systolic murmur, consistent with aortic stenosis.

stem: A patient presents with erythema migrans after a tick bite. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Key clinical clue:
•
Erythema migrans is the pathognomonic rash of early Lyme disease
Caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by the Ixodes tick.
Treatment:
•
First-line treatment for early localized Lyme disease (erythema migrans):
o
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days
•
Doxycycline is effective against Borrelia and prevents progression to:
o Neurological Lyme
o
Lyme arthritis
o
Cardiac involvement
Note:
•
If the patient is pregnant or <8 years old, doxycycline is contraindicated → use amoxicillin or
cefuroxime instead.
Conclusion:
In a patient with erythema migrans, you should start doxycycline for 21 days immediately — no
serological confirmation is needed at this early stage.

stem: A patient with joint pain and livedo reticularis is suspected to have SLE. Which antibody is most specific for SLE?
explanation:
Joint pain → common manifestation of SLE
•
Livedo reticularis → mottled, lace-like rash seen in:
o
SLE
o Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) (often secondary to SLE)
Anti-dsDNA antibody:
• Highly specific for SLE (specificity >95%)
•
Often associated with:
o
Renal involvement (lupus nephritis)
o Disease activity monitoring
•
Positive even in patients with cutaneous + joint manifestations
Other related antibodies (for understanding):
Antibody Associated with
ANA Highly sensitive but not specific for SLE
Anti-Sm Very specific but less sensitive
Anti-Ro/SSA Seen in SLE and subacute cutaneous lupus, also in neonatal lupus
Antiphospholipid (e.g., anti-
cardiolipin)
Associated with livedo reticularis, thrombosis, pregnancy loss —
important in APS, which can coexist with SLE
Conclusion:
In a case of SLE with joint pain and livedo reticularis, the most specific antibody for confirming the
diagnosis is anti-dsDNA.

stem: Asbestos exposure + exertional SOB Plural plaques (CXR) in restrictive pathology Obesity (BMI>35) KCO 106% Cause of symptoms of breathlessness?
explanation:
Key clinical findings:
•
Asbestos exposure → suggests occupational lung risk
• Exertional shortness of breath (SOB)
•
Pleural plaques on CXR → evidence of prior asbestos exposure
•
Restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing
•
KCO = 106% (normal to increased)
•
BMI >35 → significant obesity
Interpreting the pulmonary function profile:
•
Restrictive pattern + raised KCO is not typical of pulmonary fibrosis
• In pulmonary fibrosis, you expect:
o
Restriction with reduced KCO (due to thickened alveolar-capillary membrane)
•
Raised KCO suggests:
o
Reduced alveolar volume but normal or increased gas transfer per unit of lung
o
Classic in obesity (mechanical restriction, not intrinsic lung disease)
Why other options are less likely:
Option Reason
1. Pulmonary
fibrosis
Would cause restrictive pattern + low KCO
2. Pleural plaques Marker of asbestos exposure; do not impair lung function significantly
3. COPD
Causes obstructive pattern, not restrictive; KCO is usually low in emphysema-
dominant COPD
KCO (DLCO/VA) Insight:
•
Obesity causes a restrictive pattern due to chest wall/diaphragm loading.
•
Because alveolar units are preserved, KCO may be normal or elevated.
Conclusion:
In this patient with restrictive physiology, normal-to-high KCO, and morbid obesity, the most likely
cause of breathlessness is obesity, not asbestos-related lung disease.

stem: Diabetic patient, with headache, right eye downward out, and pupil drop Dx?
explanation:
Key clinical features:
• Diabetic patient
•
Headache
•
Right eye "down and out" → 3rd cranial nerve palsy
•
Pupil involvement ("pupil drop") → dilated pupil
This is a pupil-involving 3rd nerve palsy.
Differentiating causes of 3rd nerve palsy:
Feature Ischemic (e.g., diabetic) Compressive (e.g., PCOM aneurysm)
Pupil involvement Spared (outer fibers spared) Involved (pupil dilated)
Pain Possible Often sudden + painful headache
Cause Microvascular Compression (aneurysm/tumor)
Why PCOM aneurysm is correct:
•
Posterior communicating artery (PCOM) aneurysms:
o
Classically cause painful 3rd nerve palsy
o
Involve the pupil due to compression of superficial parasympathetic fibers on CN III
o
Present with "down and out" eye + dilated pupil
o Risk of rupture → subarachnoid hemorrhage if not treated
Option Why it’s incorrect
Ischemic
oculomotor palsy
Typically spares the pupil — not consistent with "pupil drop"
Cavernous
meningioma
Can affect CN III but often involves multiple cranial nerves (III, IV, V1, VI) — pupil
involvement less common early
SAH
May cause headache and CN deficits, but typically presents with sudden severe
thunderclap headache, meningeal signs, and altered consciousness
Migraine
May cause ophthalmoplegia in rare forms (e.g., ophthalmoplegic migraine), but
pupil-involving CN III palsy in a diabetic with headache is much more consistent
with aneurysm
Conclusion:
A pupil-involving 3rd nerve palsy with headache in a diabetic patient raises urgent concern for a
Posterior Communicating Artery (PCOM) aneurysm, a neurosurgical emergency.

stem: Male from Suden with ulcers on his left leg above lateral malleolus Greyish ulcer present in the calf Cause?
explanation:
(Specifically: Mycobacterium ulcerans, causing Buruli ulcer)
Key clinical clues:
•
Male from Sudan → endemic area for Buruli ulcer
•
Chronic ulcer above lateral malleolus/calf
• Greyish ulcer — classically describes the necrotic base of Buruli ulcer
Buruli Ulcer – Caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans:
•
A slowly progressive necrotizing skin infection
• Caused by toxin (mycolactone) produced by the bacteria
•
Common in tropical/subtropical regions: West Africa (e.g., Sudan), Australia
•
Often starts as a painless nodule → ulcerates over time
•
Ulcers have:
o
Undermined edges
o Necrotic (greyish) base
o
Can be painless, despite large size
Why the other options are incorrect:
Option Why it's incorrect
B. Diphtheria
Causes pharyngeal or respiratory illness; cutaneous diphtheria is rare and
not typical in this presentation
C. Rickettsia Causes febrile illnesses with rash/eschar, not large chronic ulcers
D. Pseudomonas
aeruginosa
May cause greenish wounds, especially in burns or immunocompromised,
but not a grey ulcer in this context
E. Bacillus anthracis
(Anthrax)
Painless black eschar, typically with surrounding edema, not grey ulcer and
uncommon in Sudan
Conclusion:
The chronic, greyish ulcer on the leg of a patient from Sudan is most consistent with Buruli ulcer,
caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans — making Mycobacterium the correct answer.

stem: Young man with Marfan syndrome What is frameshift mutation in FBN1 gene?
explanation:
Understanding the question:
The scenario describes a frameshift mutation in the FBN1 gene — the gene implicated in Marfan
syndrome.
What is a frameshift mutation?
•
A frameshift mutation occurs when the number of inserted or deleted nucleotides is not a
multiple of 3.
•
This alters the reading frame of the mRNA, resulting in:
o
Abnormal amino acid sequence downstream
o
Often leads to premature stop codon and truncated protein
Why "Insertion of one nucleotide" is correct:
• Inserting 1 nucleotide shifts the reading frame.
•
This disrupts the normal function of fibrillin-1, the protein encoded by FBN1.
•
Frameshift mutations are often severe and can contribute to Marfan syndrome phenotypes.
Why other options are incorrect:
Option Reason
Insertion of three
nucleotides
Does not shift the reading frame — just adds one amino acid
Deletion of 9
nucleotides
Multiple of 3 — no frameshift
Deletion of 12
nucleotides
Also multiple of 3 — no frameshift
Insertion of CAG repeat
CAG repeat expansions (e.g., Huntington's disease) cause trinucleotide
repeat disorders, not frameshift
Conclusion:
A frameshift mutation in the FBN1 gene is best represented by the insertion of one nucleotide, which
alters the reading frame and impairs production of functional fibrillin-1 — contributing to Marfan
syndrome.

stem: 43 year old man presented with complaints of headache, confusion, nausea, and vomiting. CT scan revealed inflammatory hemorrhagic changes in the bilateral temporal lobes. What is the most important initial treatment?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
• 43-year-old man
•
Symptoms: headache, confusion, nausea, vomiting → concerning for encephalitis
•
CT scan shows hemorrhagic inflammatory changes in bilateral temporal lobes
o
This is **highly characteristic of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) encephalitis, especially
HSV-1
Why Aciclovir is the most important initial treatment:
•
HSV encephalitis is a medical emergency with high morbidity and mortality if untreated.
•
Aciclovir is the antiviral of choice.
• Early initiation significantly improves outcomes — do not wait for PCR confirmation before
starting treatment.
•
Dose: typically IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours (adjust for renal function)
Why the other options are incorrect
Option Reason it’s incorrect
Amoxicillin
Not useful for viral encephalitis; more appropriate for bacterial infections (e.g., Listeria
in elderly)
Ceftriaxone Used for bacterial meningitis, not effective against HSV
Dexamethasone
Used in bacterial meningitis (e.g., pneumococcal) but not first-line in viral
encephalitis; may be considered adjunctively later in some cases
Conclusion:
A patient with bilateral temporal lobe involvement on CT and encephalopathic symptoms should be
presumed to have HSV encephalitis, and IV aciclovir must be started immediately

stem: Scenario of HSV encephalitis / rapid sodium correction. If serum Na corrected too rapidly, what complication occurs?
explanation:
Key clinical facts:
•
Sodium = 112 mmol/L → severe hyponatremia
•
Presents with drowsiness, delirium → signs of acute cerebral dysfunction due to low serum
osmolality
•
Rapid correction of sodium in chronic or severe hyponatremia is dangerous
What happens if sodium is corrected too fast?
•
Brain cells adapt to chronic hyponatremia by reducing intracellular osmolytes to avoid
swelling.
•
Rapid correction → sudden increase in plasma osmolality → water moves out of brain cells
•
This leads to:
o
Destruction of oligodendrocytes
o Demyelination, especially in the pons
Result: Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis)
Why other options are incorrect:
Option Reason
1. Cerebral
atrophy
Chronic process, not acutely caused by sodium shifts
2. Cerebral edema
Occurs in acute hyponatremia or if sodium drops too fast, not with rapid
correction
Conclusion:
In a patient with severe hyponatremia, rapid correction of sodium can lead to Osmotic Demyelination
Syndrome, a potentially irreversible and devastating complication. Sodium should be corrected slowly
and carefully.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of Fondaparinux?
options: Inhibition of Vitamin K epoxide reductase
explanation:
Mechanism of Action of Fondaparinux:
•
Fondaparinux is a synthetic pentasaccharide anticoagulant.
•
It works by binding to antithrombin III (ATIII) and selectively enhancing its activity.
•
This complex inhibits activated Factor Xa, thereby preventing the conversion of prothrombin
to thrombin
It does NOT inhibit thrombin (Factor IIa) directly.
Summary:
Feature Description
Class Synthetic indirect Factor Xa inhibitor
Target Factor Xa via antithrombin III
Effect Inhibits thrombin generation and clot formation
Use DVT, PE, post-operative thromboprophylaxis
Conclusion:
Fondaparinux acts by inhibiting Factor Xa, making that the correct and precise description of its
mechanism of action.

stem: Pt taking Rivaroxaban for AF i guess. Presented with melena PT, APTT deranged, Fibrinogen normal BP 100/70 Most appropriate management?
explanation:
Key clinical points:
•
Patient on Rivaroxaban (a direct oral anticoagulant, DOAC)
• Presents with melena → gastrointestinal bleeding
•
Deranged PT and APTT → indicates coagulopathy
•
Fibrinogen normal → no need for cryoprecipitate
• BP 100/70 → borderline hypotension, but hemodynamically stable
Why PCC (Prothrombin Complex Concentrate) is correct:
•
Rivaroxaban inhibits Factor Xa
•
In the absence of a specific reversal agent (e.g., Andexanet alfa, which is expensive and not
widely available), the recommended off-label reversal is:
4-factor PCC (contains Factors II, VII, IX, and X)
•
PCC helps restore the vitamin K–dependent clotting factors and can reverse the anticoagulant
effect of rivaroxaban.
Why the other options are incorrect:
Option Why it’s incorrect
FFP (Fresh Frozen Plasma) Not effective in reversing DOACs and requires large volumes; slower onset
Cryoprecipitate Used for low fibrinogen, which is normal in this patient
Fluid May support BP but does not address the bleeding or anticoagulation
Vitamin K Rivaroxaban is not a vitamin K antagonist → vitamin K has no effect here
Conclusion:
In a patient on Rivaroxaban presenting with GI bleeding and coagulopathy, the most appropriate
acute management is Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) to reverse the anticoagulant effect.

stem: A patient with AML presents with DIC features. Cytogenetics shows t(15;17). What is the prognosis?
options: Good prognosis — t(15;17) associated with APL, responds to ATRA
Poor prognosis — DIC indicates advanced disease
Poor prognosis — t(15;17) is an adverse marker
explanation:
Key context:
•
Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) is a well-known complication in Acute
Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL), which is a subtype of AML (M3).
•
APL is caused by the t(15;17) translocation, resulting in the PML-RARA fusion gene.
Features of t(15;17) / APL:
•
Commonly presents with:
o
Bleeding and DIC
o Pancytopenia
o
Promyelocytes with Auer rods on blood film
•
Despite the risk of life-threatening DIC, APL has a very good prognosis with prompt treatment.
Why it's good prognosis:
Highly sensitive to all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide
•
These treatments induce differentiation of promyelocytes and rapidly control coagulopathy
•
Long-term remission rates are high with modern therapy
Conclusion:
Although t(15;17) APL can present with DIC, it is actually one of the best-prognosis subtypes of AML
when diagnosed early and treated with ATRA-based regimens.

stem: Headache with 3 episodes of seizure Past history of gestational Hypertension in 3rd trimester of pregnancy Mild neck rigidity and no fever BP = Elevated What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Key clinical clues:
•
Headache (common in CVST)
•
Seizures (3 episodes) → classic presenting feature of CVST
•
History of gestational hypertension in late pregnancy → a major risk factor for
hypercoagulability
• Mild neck rigidity without fever → suggests non-infectious irritation, not meningitis
•
Elevated BP
•
No mention of fever, rash, or photophobia
Why CVT is correct:
•
Cerebral venous thrombosis is more common in:
o
Peripartum/postpartum women
o
Those with hypertension, dehydration, or thrombophilia
•
Presents with:
o
Headache (often gradual or subacute)
o
Seizures
o
Focal deficits
o Signs of raised ICP or venous infarction
•
Neck stiffness can occur due to venous congestion, even without infection
Why other options are less likely:
Diagnosis Reason it's less likely
Eclampsia
Usually occurs during or within 48 hours after delivery, with new-onset seizures,
proteinuria, and severe hypertension. Less likely here unless patient is still peripartum
SAH
Sudden thunderclap headache is typical, often with vomiting, photophobia, and altered
consciousness — less likely with seizures and no sudden onset
Meningitis
seizures also uncommon as a presenting feature in adults with meningitis
Conclusion:
In a postpartum woman with headache, seizures, mild neck rigidity, and history of gestational
hypertension, the most likely diagnosis is Cerebral Venous Thrombosis (CVT).

Needle-shaped
Negatively birefringent

Some scenario in which median free period progression was given with chemotherapy and with
supportive treatment only
Total 622 participants were studied from 6 meta-analysis
Chemo group had 8.4 weeks
Median free period progression and supportive one had 6.9 weeks
Which one represents the that?
A. Chemo give better chances of survival in gastric cancer
B. Chemo delays disease progression and death
C. 311 participants were studied in each group
D. Chemo increased survival rate
ANSWERS:
Chemo delays disease progression and death
Correct Answer: B. Chemotherapy delays disease progression and death
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Study Design: Data from 622 participants taken from 6 meta-analyses.
•
Comparison: Median progression-free survival (PFS) with:
o
Chemotherapy: 8.4 weeks
o
Supportive treatment only: 6.9 weeks
•
Focus of outcome: The metric provided is progression-free survival — this measures time until
disease worsens or death (whichever comes first).
Explanation of the Correct Answer (B):
•
Progression-Free Survival (PFS) is a direct indicator of how well a treatment delays cancer
progression and potentially prolongs life.
•
The fact that PFS is 8.4 weeks with chemo vs 6.9 weeks with supportive care indicates that
chemotherapy extends the time before the disease progresses or leads to death.
•
This does not confirm improved overall survival, but does show a delay in progression/death
— which is precisely what option B states.
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
• A. Chemo gives better chances of survival in gastric cancer
Not supported directly — overall survival data (i.e. time until death from any cause) is not
provided. Only progression-free survival is mentioned. Hence, this statement overreaches beyond
the data.
•
C. 311 participants were studied in each group
Not necessarily true — while the total is 622, there's no mention of equal allocation. The
groups could be unequal, and the scenario doesn't provide group-wise participant numbers. Thus,
this is assumptive and cannot be concluded from the information given.
• D. Chemo increased survival rate
Again, survival rate implies overall survival improvement, which is not evidenced by PFS
data alone. The trial shows delayed progression, not necessarily increased survival.

stem: 35 year old woman came with some complaints. Her elder sister had a confirmed BRCA2 mutation. Which of the following cancers is she at risk of?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Ovarian cancer
Key Points from the Scenario:
• 35-year-old woman: Young age group, where inherited cancer syndromes are often relevant.
•
Family history: Her elder sister has a confirmed BRCA2 mutation, a well-established hereditary
cancer risk gene.
•
You’re being asked to identify which cancer this woman is at increased risk of.
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Ovarian cancer):
The BRCA2 gene (Breast Cancer gene 2) is a tumor suppressor gene involved in DNA repair. Mutations
in BRCA1 or BRCA2 significantly increase the risk of:
• Breast cancer (especially early onset and bilateral forms)
•
Ovarian cancer
•
Also associated with pancreatic cancer and prostate cancer (particularly in men)
In women, ovarian cancer is one of the major malignancies linked to BRCA2 mutations, with a
substantially elevated lifetime risk compared to the general population.
Thus, this woman — as a first-degree relative of someone with a BRCA2 mutation — is at increased
genetic risk of ovarian cancer, and should be considered for genetic counseling and possibly genetic
testing.
Why the Other Option is Less Likely:
•
Gastric cancer
Although certain hereditary cancer syndromes (e.g., Lynch syndrome, CDH1 mutations in
hereditary diffuse gastric cancer) are associated with gastric cancer, BRCA2 mutations are not
classically linked to gastric cancer.
Therefore, gastric cancer is not the expected cancer risk in BRCA2 mutation carriers.

stem: A patient on long-term lithium presents with hypernatraemia, high serum osmolarity, polyuria, and urinary sodium < 20 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (DI)
Key Points from the Scenario:
• Patient on long-term lithium: Lithium is a well-known cause of nephrogenic diabetes
insipidus, especially with chronic use.
•
Hypernatremia and high serum osmolality: These are classic findings in diabetes insipidus,
due to free water loss.
•
Urinary sodium < 20 mmol/L: This suggests volume depletion — the kidneys are trying to
conserve sodium in response to hypovolemia caused by excessive water loss.
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Nephrogenic DI):
•
Diabetes insipidus is characterized by inability to concentrate urine, leading to polyuria and
dehydration.
•
In nephrogenic DI, the kidneys do not respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
•
Lithium interferes with aquaporin-2 water channels in the collecting duct, causing resistance to
ADH — this leads to nephrogenic DI.
•
Hypernatremia and high serum osmolality result from water loss exceeding sodium loss.
• Urinary sodium < 20 mmol/L indicates a volume-depleted state, where the kidney
compensates by reabsorbing sodium — but can't reabsorb water effectively due to ADH
resistance.
Why Other Conditions Are Less Likely:
•
Central DI: Would also cause hypernatremia, but is usually due to lack of ADH production.
However, in this case, lithium use strongly favors a nephrogenic (peripheral resistance)
mechanism.
•
SIADH: Would cause hyponatremia and low serum osmolality, which is the opposite here.
• Cerebral salt wasting / Addison’s disease: These can cause hyponatremia, not hypernatremia.
•
Diarrhea or vomiting: May cause low urinary sodium but would usually lead to hypo- rather than
hypernatremia unless water loss is excessive and unreplaced — still, lithium + hypernatremia
points toward DI.
MRCP Syndrome Key Clinical Pearl:
Always think of nephrogenic DI in a patient with hypernatremia + dilute urine + history of lithium
use. Early recognition is key to prevent volume depletion and complications.

stem: Pt had all the features of high prolactin. Low LH low FSH Galactorrhea Started risperidone and one other drug 1 month ago. Prolactin was in 2000s TSH = 7.5 T3 and T4 was normal No visual field defect What is the cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Risperidone
Key Clinical Features:
•
Patient has classic features of hyperprolactinemia:
o
Galactorrhea,
o Low LH and FSH (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism)
•
Prolactin level ~2000 mIU/L
•
Started risperidone + another drug 1 month ago
• TSH mildly elevated (7.5), but T3/T4 normal → Subclinical hypothyroidism
•
No visual field defects → Argues against macroadenoma/pituitary mass
Explanation of Correct Answer (Risperidone):
•
Risperidone is a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist.
o
Dopamine inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary.
o Antipsychotics like risperidone block this inhibition, resulting in elevated prolactin
levels.
•
Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia typically causes:
o
Galactorrhea, menstrual disturbance, infertility
o
Low gonadotropins (LH/FSH) due to prolactin’s suppression of GnRH
•
Prolactin levels in the 1000–3000 range are common with risperidone and do not necessarily
indicate a prolactinoma.
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
•
Prolactinoma
Prolactin levels >5000 mIU/L are more suggestive.
Prolactin in the 2000s + recent antipsychotic use + no visual symptoms favors drug-
induced cause.
•
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism can cause modest hyperprolactinemia via TRH stimulation, but prolactin
rarely exceeds 50–100 μg/L (≈1000–2000 mIU/L)
Also, TSH is only mildly raised with normal T3/T4 → subclinical hypothyroidism, unlikely to
be the primary cause.
Clinical Pearl:
•
In patients on dopamine antagonists (e.g., risperidone), always consider drug-induced
hyperprolactinemia first.
• Prolactin <3000 mIU/L + normal MRI = likely drug-induced
•
Prolactin >5000 mIU/L or visual symptoms = consider prolactinoma

stem: 43 female with recurrent abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea. She was taking ibuprofen for long standing joint pain. In the past she has been investigated for primary infertility. Despite stopping ibuprofen and taking omeprazole for 6 weeks her GI symptoms has not improved. Bloods: Hb 122 adj Calcium 2.88 high phosphate normal albumin normal CRP 10 UGIE: multiple duodenal ulcers Biopsy: H pylori Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer: d) MEN (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia – likely MEN1/Zollinger-Ellison syndrome)
Key Clinical Clues in the Scenario:
Recurrent abdominal pain + watery diarrhoea → Suggests secretory diarrhoea or high acid
output.
•
Multiple duodenal ulcers on UGIE → Red flag for Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma).
• No response to omeprazole and ibuprofen stopped → Makes NSAID-related ulcer unlikely.
•
H. pylori positive → Common, but unlikely to cause multiple ulcers or severe secretory
diarrhoea.
•
Hypercalcemia (Ca = 2.88 mmol/L) → Significant clue; unexplained hypercalcemia + ulcers
points toward MEN1.
• Past history of primary infertility → May hint at endocrine abnormality (e.g., pituitary
involvement in MEN1).
•
CRP = 10 → Mild inflammation but not enough to support IBD or lymphoma definitively.
Explanation of Correct Answer (d) MEN):
•
MEN type 1 (Wermer’s syndrome) involves:
o
Parathyroid adenomas → hypercalcemia
o
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors → e.g., gastrinoma → Zollinger–Ellison syndrome
(ZE)
o Pituitary tumors → Can cause infertility (e.g., prolactinoma)
•
Zollinger–Ellison syndrome causes:
o
Multiple duodenal ulcers
o
Watery diarrhoea due to gastric acid hypersecretion
o
Poor response to PPIs alone in severe cases
o
Often associated with MEN1 when part of a syndromic picture (especially with
hypercalcemia)
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
• a) Crohn’s disease
Can cause diarrhoea and abdominal pain, but multiple duodenal ulcers and hypercalcemia
are not typical. Also, CRP is only mildly elevated.
• b) Cushing's syndrome
Can cause abdominal symptoms and infertility, but does not typically cause duodenal ulcers
or high calcium. Would expect features like weight gain, hypertension, striae.
•
c) Ibuprofen-induced ulcers
NSAIDs cause single or few gastric/duodenal ulcers, not multiple refractory ones. Symptoms
persisted despite stopping ibuprofen and using PPI.
•
e) Small bowel lymphoma
Might cause abdominal pain and diarrhoea, but ulcers, hypercalcemia, and infertility history
are not characteristic. No weight loss or systemic signs mentioned.
Clinical Pearl:
In a patient with multiple duodenal ulcers, watery diarrhoea, and hypercalcemia, always consider
MEN1 with gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome).

stem: 58 female with Rheumatoid arthritis and CKD on regular dialysis came with severe bone pain. Bloods: Adj Calcium low , phosphate normal , albumin mild low ALP raised PTH raised What is the Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer: e) Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
58-year-old female with:
o
Rheumatoid arthritis
o
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) on regular dialysis
o
Severe bone pain
•
Blood results:
o
Adjusted calcium: low
o
Phosphate: normal
o Albumin: mildly low
o
ALP: raised
o
PTH: raised
Explanation of the Correct Answer (e) Secondary Hyperparathyroidism):
•
In CKD, the kidneys fail to:
o Excrete phosphate → may lead to hyperphosphatemia
o
Activate vitamin D → leads to reduced calcium absorption from gut
•
This results in hypocalcemia, which stimulates parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion — causing
secondary hyperparathyroidism.
•
PTH increases bone turnover to raise calcium levels, leading to:
o
Bone pain
o
Raised ALP (marker of increased bone remodeling)
•
These changes are part of renal osteodystrophy, particularly the osteitis fibrosa cystica subtype.
So, in a dialysis-dependent CKD patient with:
Low calcium
•
Raised PTH
•
Raised ALP
• Bone pain
→ The most likely diagnosis is secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
•
a) Dialysis-related amyloidosis
Typically causes carpal tunnel syndrome, joint pain, and shoulder pad sign, not classic for
low calcium or raised PTH.
•
b) Osteomalacia
Would cause low phosphate and low or normal PTH unless due to CKD. Also associated
with vitamin D deficiency (more likely in non-dialysis patients).
•
c) Osteoporosis
Not associated with raised ALP or PTH. Osteoporosis has normal labs, and pain is usually
from fractures, not diffuse.
• d) Paget’s disease
Causes very high ALP but normal calcium and PTH. Also tends to be focal (e.g. skull, pelvis),
not diffuse pain in a dialysis patient.
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearl:
In CKD or dialysis patients with bone pain, always consider secondary hyperparathyroidism if calcium
is low and PTH/ALP are raised.

stem: A patient is about to begin anti-TNF therapy. Which test must be checked to screen for latent tuberculosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA)
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
The patient is about to begin anti-TNF therapy.
•
Anti-TNF agents (e.g., infliximab, etanercept, adalimumab) suppress immune function,
particularly TNF-α, which is critical in containing latent tuberculosis (TB).
•
Reactivation of latent TB is a well-known and serious complication of anti-TNF therapy.
Explanation of the Correct Answer (IGRA):
•
IGRA is the preferred test for detecting latent TB infection (LTBI) in patients who:
o
Are immunosuppressed or about to be immunosuppressed
o
Have received BCG vaccination (to avoid false positives from TST)
o
Need a single-visit test (no return for reading like TST)
•
Why screen for TB before anti-TNF?
o TNF-α is essential for granuloma maintenance that walls off latent TB.
o
Suppressing TNF can lead to breakdown of granulomas and reactivation of TB.
o
IGRA is more specific than TST and not affected by BCG status — making it ideal in this
setting.
Why Other Tests (if listed) Would Be Less Appropriate:
•
TST (Mantoux test)
Can give false positives in BCG-vaccinated patients. Also requires return visit.
•
Chest X-ray
May be added to rule out active TB if IGRA is positive — but not used alone to screen for
latent infection.
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearl:
▪ Always perform TB screening (preferably with IGRA) before starting any biologic
immunosuppressive therapy like anti-TNF agents.

stem: Sharp chest pain and left arm numbness in a 43 years old F smoker with a family history of IHD Best modality to investigate?
explanation:
Correct Answer: CT angiography
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
43-year-old female
•
Smoker, family history of ischaemic heart disease (IHD)
•
Symptoms: Sharp chest pain and left arm numbness
•
High-risk features:
o
Young female with cardiovascular risk factors (smoking, family history)
o
Symptoms possibly cardiac, vascular, or even aortic in origin
Explanation of the Correct Answer (CT Angiography):
•
In a patient with atypical chest pain, radiation to the arm, and risk factors for coronary artery
disease (CAD), you must rule out serious vascular causes:
o
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS)
o
Aortic dissection
o
Pulmonary embolism (PE) (though less likely without dyspnoea or hypoxia)
• CT coronary angiography is the non-invasive gold standard to assess:
o
Coronary artery anatomy
o
Aortic abnormalities
o
Can quickly exclude CAD or dissection in high-risk symptomatic individuals
•
It's particularly useful in intermediate-risk patients where traditional ECG/troponin are
inconclusive, and you want to exclude coronary pathology definitively.
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
MR scan (Cardiac MRI)
Useful for myocarditis, cardiomyopathies, infarct sizing, but not the first-line for acute
chest pain with concern for ACS or vascular causes.
• Echocardiography
Good for assessing valvular disease, pericardial effusion, LV function, but not sensitive
enough for coronary artery disease or aortic dissection, especially if chest pain is sharp and
unexplained.
•
PET-CT
Used for metabolic imaging, e.g. to assess viable myocardium or malignancy, not for
acute chest pain work-up.
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearl:
In a patient with chest pain and vascular risk factors, CT angiography is the best non-invasive tool to
exclude coronary artery disease and aortic pathology in one scan.

stem: An HIV patient presents with purpuric/violaceous lesions on the upper body. Kaposi sarcoma is suspected. What is the causative agent?
explanation:
Correct Answer: HHV-8 (Human Herpesvirus 8)
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
HIV-positive patient
•
Purpuric lesions on the upper body
• Clinical suspicion of Kaposi sarcoma, a common AIDS-defining malignancy
Explanation of the Correct Answer (HHV-8):
• Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi
Sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV).
•
It presents with:
o
Violaceous or purpuric skin lesions (can affect trunk, limbs, face, oral mucosa)
o
Can involve lymph nodes, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract
• HHV-8 infects endothelial cells, leading to angioproliferative tumors — which explains the
vascular appearance of the lesions.
•
KS is more aggressive and widespread in immunocompromised individuals, especially in AIDS
patients with low CD4 counts.
Differential (not correct in this context):
•
HIV itself does not directly cause KS
•
Other viruses (e.g., EBV, CMV, HSV) may cause other complications but are not the cause of
Kaposi sarcoma
Clinical Pearl:
In any HIV patient with purple vascular skin lesions, think Kaposi sarcoma and HHV-8 as the cause —
especially if CD4 < 200.

stem: Where is CSF produced vs absorbed? The question asks about CSF absorption site.
explanation:
Absorption = Arachnoid granulations (Sagittal sinus)
Correct Answer: Sagittal sinus
(Specifically, arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus)
Key Points:
•
The question asks where cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is absorbed, not where it's produced.
• Common confusion exists between production (choroid plexus) and absorption (arachnoid
granulations).
•
Among the listed options, we need to identify the correct anatomical site for CSF reabsorption.
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Sagittal sinus):
•
CSF is primarily absorbed into the venous system via arachnoid granulations, which are small
projections of arachnoid mater into the superior sagittal sinus — a large venous channel in the
dura mater.
•
This absorption is pressure-dependent and ensures proper CSF circulation and intracranial
pressure regulation.
So, while the arachnoid granulations are the direct absorptive structures, the superior sagittal sinus (a
dural venous sinus) is the site where CSF drains into — making "sagittal sinus" the best choice among
the given options.
Why the Other Option Is Incorrect:
•
Choroid plexus
This is the site of CSF production, not absorption. The choroid plexus, located within the
ventricles (especially the lateral, third, and fourth), secretes CSF through active transport
mechanisms.
Clinical relevance:
•
Impaired absorption at the arachnoid granulations (e.g., after meningitis or SAH) can lead to
communicating hydrocephalus.
• Blockage before absorption (e.g., aqueductal stenosis) causes non-communicating
hydrocephalu

stem: Asymptomatic patient had BCG vaccination, tuberculin strongly positive (more than 15mm) What would be the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Do nothing
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Asymptomatic patient: No signs or symptoms of active TB.
•
History of BCG vaccination
•
Strongly positive tuberculin skin test (TST): >15 mm
•
The question is asking about the appropriate next step — i.e., whether this result warrants
treatment for latent TB or not.
Explanation of the Correct Answer ("Do nothing"):
•
A tuberculin skin test (TST) can be falsely positive in patients who previously received BCG,
especially if the induration is <15 mm.
•
However, even a >15 mm TST in a BCG-vaccinated, asymptomatic patient without risk
factors for TB exposure does not automatically require treatment.
Most guidelines (e.g. CDC, NICE, WHO) recommend that:
TST results should be interpreted in context:
▪
15 mm is considered positive in any person, but in low-risk, BCG-vaccinated,
asymptomatic individuals, further steps depend on risk of exposure or
conversion, not TST alone.
o
Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRA) (e.g. Quantiferon-TB Gold) are preferred in
BCG-vaccinated individuals to avoid false positives.
•
Since this patient is asymptomatic, previously BCG-vaccinated, and no risk factors are
mentioned, the positive TST alone does not indicate latent TB that needs treatment.
Why the Other Option is Less Likely:
•
Latent TB treatment
Would be appropriate only if there’s a high risk of TB exposure, conversion, or
immunocompromised status, or if IGRA is positive in BCG-vaccinated patients.
TST alone is not sufficient to diagnose latent TB in someone with prior BCG vaccination
unless additional risk factors exist or IGRA confirms.
•
BAL (Bronchoalveolar lavage)
Invasive test reserved for diagnosing active pulmonary TB in symptomatic or radiologically
suspicious patients.
Not appropriate in asymptomatic individuals.
Clinical Pearl:
In BCG-vaccinated individuals, use IGRA to confirm latent TB before initiating treatment — especially
in low-risk, asymptomatic patients.

stem: Farmer started complaining of Raynaud like symptoms All immune markers were normal Anti centromere negative, ANA negative Most likely cause of symptoms?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Vibrating tool
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Farmer with Raynaud-like symptoms
• All autoimmune markers negative
ANA: Negative
o
Anti-centromere: Negative
•
Looking for a non-autoimmune cause of Raynaud’s phenomenon in an occupational setting.
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Vibrating tool):
•
This is a classic presentation of vibration-induced vasospastic symptoms, often called:
o Hand-arm vibration syndrome (HAVS) or
o
Occupational Raynaud’s
•
It results from prolonged use of vibrating tools such as:
o Jackhammers, chainsaws, or powered farming equipment
•
The repetitive vibration exposure causes damage to digital blood vessels and nerves, leading
to:
o
Blanching of fingers, numbness, tingling
o
Raynaud-like attacks precipitated by cold or vibration
Autoimmune markers are negative, supporting a secondary, non-autoimmune cause — especially
relevant in farmers or manual laborers.
Why the Other Option Is Less Likely:
•
OPC (Organophosphate) poisoning
Causes cholinergic toxidrome, not Raynaud-like vasospasm
Features include:
o
SLUDGE syndrome (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Diarrhea, GI upset, Emesis)
o
Bradycardia, miosis, muscle fasciculations
No vascular spasm or white finger symptoms as seen in Raynaud’s
Clinical Pearl:
In manual laborers or farmers with Raynaud-like symptoms and negative autoimmune tests,
consider vibration exposure as a cause — especially if they use powered tools frequently.

stem: A patient presents with resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity. Degeneration of which structure is responsible for Parkinson's disease?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Substantia nigra
Cause of Parkinson’s Disease:
•
Parkinson’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder caused primarily by the progressive loss
of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta — a part of the basal ganglia
in the midbrain.
•
The substantia nigra produces dopamine, which is critical for:
o
Regulating movement
o Coordinating smooth and purposeful motor activity
Pathological Hallmarks:
•
Dopamine deficiency → disrupts balance between excitatory and inhibitory pathways in the basal
ganglia.
•
Presence of Lewy bodies (intracellular inclusions containing α-synuclein).
Classic Parkinson's Symptoms (TRAP):
Symptom Explanation
Tremor Resting tremor, “pill-rolling”
Rigidity Cogwheel rigidity
Akinesia/Bradykinesia Slowness of movement, masked face
Postural instability Impaired balance, frequent falls
WPW syndrome with accessory pathway defect
Which interval will be effected on ECG?
1. QT
2. QRS
3. PR
ANSWERS:
PR
Correct Answer: 3. PR
Key Concept: Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW) Syndrome
• WPW syndrome is caused by an accessory conduction pathway (Bundle of Kent) that bypasses
the AV node, allowing early depolarization of the ventricles.
•
This leads to characteristic ECG findings.
ECG Findings in WPW:
ECG Feature Mechanism
Short PR interval Due to early conduction through accessory pathway (bypasses AV node)
Delta wave Slurred upstroke of QRS — from early but slow ventricular activation
Widened QRS Due to fusion of normal and accessory pathway conduction
But the hallmark abnormality and earliest sign is the shortened PR interval
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
•
1. QT interval
QT is not primarily affected in WPW syndrome.
•
2. QRS interval
QRS may be widened, but not as consistently or characteristically as PR shortening. The
delta wave broadens the QRS, but the PR shortening is the earliest and most specific change.
Clinical Summary:
In WPW syndrome, the PR interval is shortened due to pre-excitation via the accessory pathway.
