Man with Haemophilia A + Wife carrier
Percentage of daughters with disease?
ANSWERS:
50%
Correct Answer: 50% of daughters will be carriers, 0% will have the disease
Key Genetics Recap:
• Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder.
•
The father has Haemophilia A → genotype: XʰY
•
The mother is a carrier → genotype: XʰX
We need to determine the probability of daughters being affected vs carriers.
Possible Offspring Outcomes:
Father's gametes Xʰ (affected X) Y (male)
Mother's gametes X (normal) Xʰ (carrier X)
Daughters:
•
Xʰ (father) + X (mother) = XʰX → Carrier daughter
•
Xʰ (father) + Xʰ (mother) = XʰXʰ → Affected daughter
So:
•
50% of daughters = XʰX → Carriers
• 50% of daughters = XʰXʰ → Affected
BUT this is only theoretically possible — now here's the key clinical point.
Clinical Clarification:
In X-linked recessive conditions like Haemophilia A:
•
Females with two affected X chromosomes (XʰXʰ) can be affected.
•
But this is extremely rare in real life and often incompatible with normal clotting, so the term
“affected” usually refers to males.
•
However, since this daughter would inherit one affected X from the father and one from a
carrier mother, theoretically, 50% of daughters could have Haemophilia A.
Therefore, final answer:
•
50% of daughters = carriers (XʰX)
•
50% of daughters = affected (XʰXʰ) → but rare, may vary in severity due to lyonisation (X-
inactivation)
Genetic Risk Terms:
• 50% of daughters will be affected by Haemophilia A, 50% will be carriers.
If you were asking specifically about carriers, then:
Answer: 50% of daughters will be carriers.

stem: A 45 year old patient with diabetic nephropathy develops new onset hypertension. Which antihypertensive is most appropriate?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Losartan
Key Clinical Clues:
•
45-year-old with diabetic nephropathy
• New-onset hypertension
•
You’re asked to choose the most appropriate antihypertensive agent
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Losartan):
•
Losartan is an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB).
•
In diabetic nephropathy, the goal is not just BP control but also renal protection.
•
ARBs (like losartan) and ACE inhibitors:
o
Lower intraglomerular pressure
o Reduce proteinuria
o
Slow progression of diabetic kidney disease
•
Guidelines (e.g., NICE, ADA, KDIGO) recommend:
ACE inhibitors or ARBs as first-line antihypertensives in patients with diabetes and
albuminuria (i.e., nephropathy)
Why Other Antihypertensives Are Less Preferred Initially:
•
Calcium channel blockers (CCBs): Effective for BP, but less effective for renal protection or
proteinuria reduction.
• Thiazides: May worsen glycemic control and are less effective in CKD with GFR < 30.
•
Beta-blockers: Not first-line for diabetic nephropathy, may mask hypoglycemia.
•
ACE inhibitors: Equally appropriate as losartan; if patient had ACE intolerance (e.g., cough),
losartan is the better choice.
Clinical Pearl:
In diabetic patients with nephropathy, choose an ARB or ACE inhibitor — even if BP is only mildly
elevated — for dual benefit: BP control and renal protection.

stem: One question about heart failure (DCM) Breathless after walking a few steps + Climbing stairs Already on bisoprolol, ramipril, and furosemide but no improvement after 5 days Investigations normal No signs of cardiac failure What would be the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Continue same treatment / Do nothing
Key Clinical Clues:
•
Patient with DCM (dilated cardiomyopathy) and heart failure symptoms:
o
Breathlessness on exertion (e.g. stairs, walking a few steps)
• Already on appropriate heart failure therapy:
o
Bisoprolol (β-blocker)
o
Ramipril (ACE inhibitor)
o Furosemide (loop diuretic)
•
No signs of fluid overload or decompensated heart failure
•
Investigations normal
•
No improvement, but only after 5 days of therapy
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Continue same treatment / Do nothing):
•
Heart failure medications (especially β-blockers and ACE inhibitors) take weeks to months to
show clinical improvement.
•
Diuretics (like furosemide) offer symptomatic relief, but they do not improve mortality.
•
No signs of fluid overload → no immediate need to escalate diuretics.
•
Only 5 days of treatment is too short to assess full therapeutic benefit.
•
Escalating or changing medications prematurely can cause harm or confound assessment.
Therefore, the most appropriate step is to continue current therapy and reassess response after more
time.
Why Other Options Are Less Appropriate:
•
Add bendroflumethiazide
Not indicated unless resistant fluid overload; no benefit in euvolemic patients.
•
Increase dose of furosemide
No signs of congestion/fluid overload; increasing loop diuretics in this setting may cause
hypovolemia, renal impairment, or electrolyte imbalance.
•
Add digoxin
Digoxin is reserved for:
o
Heart failure with atrial fibrillation, or
o
Symptomatic HFrEF despite optimal therapy, typically after optimizing ACEi/ARB/β-
blocker/MRA.
Not appropriate this early
Clinical Pearl:
In stable heart failure patients, allow sufficient time (several weeks) for standard therapies to work
before making changes — unless signs of deterioration or fluid overload develop.

stem: A patient is diagnosed with lichen planus (treated with clobetasol propionate). What is the pathognomonic feature?
explanation:
Correct Answer Summary:
•
Diagnosis: Classic Lichen Planus
• Treatment: Clobetasol propionate (a potent topical corticosteroid)
•
Pathognomonic feature: Oral involvement (e.g., Wickham’s striae)
Explanation of Key Points:
Lichen Planus Overview:
• Chronic inflammatory skin condition involving:
o
Skin → Violaceous, flat-topped, polygonal papules
o
Mucous membranes (especially oral mucosa)
o Nails and scalp (can lead to scarring alopecia)
Key Clinical Features – “6 P’s” of Lichen Planus:
Feature Description
Pruritic Often intensely itchy
Purple Violaceous/purplish hue
Polygonal Angular borders
Planar Flat-topped papules
Papules Small, discrete lesions
Plaques Can coalesce into larger lesions
Pathognomonic Feature: Oral Involvement
•
Oral lichen planus is considered pathognomonic.
•
Classic finding: Wickham’s striae — fine white lacy pattern on buccal mucosa or tongue.
•
Often asymptomatic, but can cause burning, soreness, or erosions.
First-Line Treatment: Clobetasol Propionate
•
A very potent topical corticosteroid
• Used for:
o
Cutaneous lichen planus
o
Oral lichen planus (as a gel/ointment or mouthwash)
•
Help reduce inflammation and relieve symptoms

stem: Which of the following is a recognised adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Glycosuria
Explanation:
•
SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) are sodium-glucose co-
transporter 2 inhibitors.
• They act by blocking glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubules, leading to:
o
Increased urinary glucose excretion
o
⟶ This causes glycosuria.
Key Adverse Effects of SGLT2 Inhibitors:
Adverse Effect Explanation
Glycosuria
Therapeutic and expected effect — due to reduced glucose
reabsorption
Genital infections Especially fungal (candida) due to glucose in urine
UTIs Increased glucose in urine can encourage bacterial growth
Hypotension Osmotic diuresis can reduce blood pressure
DKA (euglycemic DKA) Rare but serious — especially during acute illness or surgery
Volume depletion
Osmotic diuresis can lead to dehydration, especially in the
elderly
Lower limb amputation
(canagliflozin)
Observed in some studies; less clear for other agents
Clinical Pearl:
▪ Glycosuria is not a side effect, but an intended pharmacological action of SGLT2 inhibitors —
it’s the mechanism behind their glucose-lowering effect.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of statins?
explanation:
Correct Answer: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors
Mechanism of Action of Statins:
•
Statins work by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in the cholesterol
biosynthesis pathway.
•
This enzyme normally converts:
HMG-CoA → Mevalonate → Cholesterol synthesis
•
By blocking this step:
o
Hepatic cholesterol synthesis is reduced
o LDL receptor expression increases
o
This leads to increased clearance of LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream
Clinical Pearl:
Statins are first-line agents for reducing cardiovascular risk by lowering LDL-C and have additional
pleiotropic effects (e.g., improving endothelial function, stabilizing plaques, anti-inflammatory actions).

stem: Pt had history of malnutrition and alcoholism Had diarrhea and a symmetrical rash on his upper torso / limb Sometimes depression and also there is dermatitis present in the axilla Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Vitamin B3 class deficiency (Niacin deficiency – Pellagra)
Key Clinical Clues:
•
History of malnutrition and alcoholism
→ Strong risk factor for B-vitamin deficiencies, especially B3 (niacin)
•
Diarrhea + Dermatitis + Depression
→ Classic triad of Pellagra (3 D’s)
• Symmetrical rash on upper torso/limbs, axillary dermatitis
→ Suggests photosensitive and distributional dermatitis, characteristic of niacin deficiency
Explanation of Correct Answer (Vitamin B3 deficiency – Pellagra):
• Niacin (Vitamin B3) is essential for NAD/NADP synthesis.
•
Deficiency leads to:
o
Dermatitis (photosensitive, often symmetric, affecting sun-exposed areas and flexures like
axilla)
o
Diarrhea
o
Dementia/depression
o
If untreated → Death
•
Seen in:
o Alcoholism
o
Malnutrition
o
Hartnup disease
o
Isoniazid or carcinoid syndrome
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
• Vitamin B1 (Thiamine)
Causes Wernicke-Korsakoff, beriberi – neurological + cardiac signs, not diarrhea or rash
•
Vitamin B7 (Biotin)
Causes dermatitis, alopecia, but diarrhea and symmetrical sun-exposed rash not typical
•
Vitamin B12
Causes macrocytic anemia, neuropathy, glossitis, not dermatitis or diarrhea
•
Folate deficiency
Causes macrocytic anemia, neural tube defects, but no skin or GI findings like in this case
Clinical Pearl:
Pellagra = 3 D’s: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia
Think of niacin deficiency (B3) in any alcoholic or malnourished patient with rash + neuropsychiatric
• GI symptoms.

stem: A patient had a diagnosis of WPW with narrow complex tachycardia What is the site of action of adenosine?
explanation:
Correct Answer: AV node
Explanation:
•
Adenosine is an ultrashort-acting AV nodal blocking agent.
•
It works by:
o
Activating adenosine receptors in the AV node
o Causing transient AV nodal block, which interrupts reentrant tachycardias that depend
on the AV node.
Site of Action of Adenosine:
Structure Adenosine Action
AV node Primary site of action – slows or blocks conduction
Accessory pathway (e.g., in WPW) No direct action
Atria/Ventricles Minimal effect
Important Clinical Note in WPW:
•
In WPW syndrome with AVRT (atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia) and narrow complex
tachycardia, the circuit involves the AV node, so adenosine is effective.
•
However, if the patient has atrial fibrillation with WPW → avoid adenosine, as it may block
the AV node and allow rapid conduction via the accessory pathway, leading to ventricular
fibrillation.
Summary:
Adenosine acts at the AV node, not the accessory pathway, and is effective in narrow-complex AV
node–dependent tachycardias, including orthodromic AVRT in WPW.

stem: What is the first-line topical treatment for lichen planus?
explanation:
Patient had an MI.
After few hours of PCI he developed palpitations’
BP was 110/70 mmHg
He had no signs of heart failure
[The patient’s condition deteriorated?????????]
ECG was done which showed "Broad QRS complexes with no p waves” + Heart Rate 103 bpm
Most appropriate treatment?
1. Electrical cardioversion
2. Amiodarone
3. Lignocaine
4. Bisoprolol
5. Verapamil
ANSWERS:
Amiodarone
Correct Answer: 2. Amiodarone
Key Clinical Scenario Summary:
•
Recent MI + palpitations a few hours after PCI
•
Hemodynamically stable initially (BP 110/70)
•
No signs of heart failure
•
ECG:
o
Broad QRS complexes
o
No visible P waves
o
Heart rate = 103 bpm
Interpretation:
•
This is most consistent with ventricular tachycardia (VT):
o Broad complex rhythm
o
No P waves
o
Slightly elevated HR (>100 bpm)
•
Post-MI patients are at high risk for ventricular arrhythmias, especially monomorphic VT.
Why Amiodarone is the Best Choice:
• Amiodarone is the first-line antiarrhythmic in stable ventricular tachycardia, especially in
post-MI patients.
•
It:
o
Suppresses ventricular arrhythmias
o
Has less negative inotropic effect than other antiarrhythmics
•
Dose: Typically 300 mg IV over 20–60 minutes, followed by infusion.
Why Other Options Are Less Appropriate:
•
1. Electrical cardioversion
Reserved for hemodynamically unstable VT (e.g. hypotension, chest pain, loss of
consciousness).
This patient is stable, so chemical cardioversion is preferred initially.
•
2. Lignocaine
Older agent used for ischemic VT, but less effective than amiodarone and not first-line now.
•
3. Bisoprolol (beta-blocker)
Not used in acute management of VT. May worsen VT acutely due to negative inotropy.
•
4. Verapamil
Contraindicated in VT — can cause hemodynamic collapse in wide-complex tachycardia.
Clinical Pearl:
In post-MI patients with a broad complex tachycardia and no shock or HF, start with IV amiodarone
to control ventricular tachycardia safely and effectively.

stem: A 35 year old lady developed hypothyroidism (constipation, lethargy). Had throat pain 1 month ago. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies mildly elevated. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: 1. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
Key Clinical Clues:
•
35-year-old woman
•
Symptoms of hypothyroidism: lethargy, constipation
Throat pain 1 month ago → possibly viral, now resolved
•
Current thyroid function tests:
o
Low T3, T4
o High TSH → Primary hypothyroidism
•
Anti-TPO (thyroid peroxidase antibody) positive
Explanation of the Correct Answer (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis):
•
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is a chronic autoimmune thyroid disease.
•
Hallmarks:
o Anti-TPO antibodies (seen in >90%)
o
Primary hypothyroidism: High TSH + low T3/T4
o
Often seen in young to middle-aged women
•
Patients may have a history of painless thyroiditis, sometimes preceded by transient
hyperthyroid phase (Hashitoxicosis).
•
The presence of anti-TPO positivity + overt hypothyroidism confirms the diagnosis.
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
•
2. De Quervain’s (subacute granulomatous) thyroiditis
Classically presents with painful thyroid and initial hyperthyroid phase, not primary
hypothyroidism.
May follow viral illness but not associated with anti-TPO antibodies.
Usually shows low TSH and high T3/T4 initially, followed later by transient hypothyroidism.
•
3. Graves’ disease
Causes hyperthyroidism → low TSH, high T3/T4
Associated with TSH receptor antibodies, not anti-TPO positivity alone.
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearl:
Anti-TPO + hypothyroidism = Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
Especially in a middle-aged woman with no signs of active inflammation, this is the classic
presentation.

stem: In a long randomized trial, some patients dropped out midway. Researchers decided to include these patients in the analysis regardless of whether they completed the study. What analysis is this?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis
Explanation:
• Intention-to-treat (ITT) is a principle used in analyzing randomized controlled trials (RCTs),
where:
All participants are analyzed in the groups to which they were originally assigned,
regardless of whether they completed the intervention or adhered to the protocol.
•
In your scenario:
o
Some patients dropped out of the study (non-compliance, withdrawal, etc.)
o
Researchers still included their data in the final analysis
→ This is a classic application of the ITT principle.
Why ITT Is Important:
•
Preserves the benefits of randomization
•
Reflects real-world effectiveness (not just efficacy)
•
Prevents selection bias that could arise if non-completers are excluded
•
Provides a conservative estimate of treatment effect
Contrasted with:
Approach Description
Per-protocol analysis Includes only participants who fully followed the study protocol
As-treated analysis Groups participants based on the treatment they actually received
Summary:
Including all randomized patients, even those who dropped out or didn’t follow the protocol =
Intention-to-treat analysis

stem: A 56 year old patient had a biopsy for colorectal cancer. Family history of early onset colorectal cancer. Biopsy shows which type of polyp predisposing to CRC in Lynch syndrome?
explanation:
Correct Answer: 1. Adenomatous
Explanation:
•
The patient has:
o
100 colorectal polyps
o
Family history of early-onset colorectal cancer
o
APC gene mutation
This is classic for Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP), an autosomal dominant condition caused
by mutations in the APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) gene.
Histological Type of Polyps in FAP:
Adenomatous polyps are the hallmark of FAP:
o
Tubular, villous, or tubulovillous adenomas
o Dysplastic and premalignant
o
High risk of transformation into adenocarcinoma if not prophylactically managed
Why Option 2 (Hamartomatous) Is Incorrect:
•
Hamartomatous polyps are seen in other syndromes, not FAP:
o
Peutz–Jeghers syndrome
o Juvenile polyposis
•
These polyps are generally non-dysplastic, though cancer risk may still be increased in some
syndromes
Summary:
▪ In FAP, polyps are adenomatous in histology — dysplastic and premalignant.
Caused by APC mutation, with hundreds to thousands of polyps often appearing in the second
or third decade.

stem: A patient developed wide spread itch. On examination he had nodular lesions in axilla and groin. He also had grey tracks on his palms. Most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Correct Answer: 4. Topical permethrin
Explanation:
•
The patient presents with widespread itching, nodular lesions in warm/moist areas (axilla and
groin), and most importantly, grey burrow-like tracks on the palms — this is classic for scabies
Scabies is caused by infestation with the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, which burrows into the skin and
causes intense pruritus, especially at night.
•
Burrows on palms and nodules in skin folds are highly suggestive.
First-line treatment:
•
Topical permethrin 5% cream is the first-line treatment for scabies:
o Applied to entire body (including under fingernails and scalp in some cases) and left
overnight (8–14 hours).
o
Repeat application after 7 days to kill any newly hatched mites.
o Treat all household contacts simultaneously.
Why Other Options Are Less Appropriate:
•
1. Clobetasol propionate
Potent steroid — may reduce inflammation but does not treat the underlying infestation.
•
2. Oral prednisolone
Immunosuppressive — contraindicated in active parasitic infection and may worsen the
condition.
•
3. Topical ivermectin
Not standard. Oral ivermectin may be used in resistant or crusted scabies, but topical
ivermectin is not first-line.
Clinical Pearl:
▪ In scabies, the most important clue is burrows and intense nocturnal itching, particularly in the
web spaces, axilla, groin, and palms.
▪ Treat with topical permethrin 5% and ensure contact prophylaxis.

stem: A patient presents with polyuria, lethargy and abdominal pain. pH = 7.15, ketones elevated. DKA is diagnosed. Which is the predominant ketone responsible?
explanation:
Correct Answer: 2. β-hydroxybutyrate
Explanation:
In Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), the body shifts into ketone production due to absolute or relative
insulin deficiency, resulting in the accumulation of ketone bodies which cause metabolic acidosis.
The three primary ketone bodies are:
3. β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB)
4. Acetoacetate
5. Acetone (least clinically significant, exhaled as fruity breath)
Among these, in DKA, the predominant ketone produced is:
β-hydroxybutyrate, especially during:
•
Severe insulin deficiency
•
Hypoperfusion or hypoxia (more reduced NAD⁺/NADH ratio)
This is why serum β-hydroxybutyrate is the most accurate test to detect and monitor ketone levels in
DKA.
Why Acetoacetate Is Less Likely:
•
Acetoacetate is also a ketone, but:
o
It is less abundant than BHB during acute DKA.
o Standard urine dipstick tests detect acetoacetate, but may underestimate severity
because they don’t detect β-hydroxybutyrate
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearl:
▪ In DKA, β-hydroxybutyrate is the dominant ketone and primary contributor to metabolic
acidosis — making it the true culprit.

stem: A 72 year old patient presented with diarrhea and left iliac fossa pain. He had history of constipation. On examination, he was had tenderness in left iliac fossa. No mass was palpable. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: 2. Diverticulitis
Explanation:
This is a classic presentation of diverticulitis, particularly involving the sigmoid colon, which is the most
commonly affected site.
Key Clinical Clues:
•
Elderly patient (72 years old)
•
Left iliac fossa (LIF) pain + tenderness
•
History of constipation (common in diverticulosis)
• Now presents with diarrhea and LIF pain
•
No mass palpable (so likely uncomplicated diverticulitis)
Why Diverticulitis Fits Best:
•
Diverticulosis = outpouchings of the colonic mucosa, often asymptomatic
•
Diverticulitis = inflammation/infection of a diverticulum, presenting with:
o
LIF pain
o
Diarrhea or altered bowel habits
o +/- Fever, raised WBC, CRP
•
Common in elderly, low-fiber diets, chronic constipation
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
•
1. Sigmoid volvulus
Usually causes abdominal distension, obstipation, and vomiting, not LIF tenderness with
diarrhea.
•
2. Carcinoma
Can mimic diverticulitis but often has insidious onset, weight loss, and altered bowel habits,
and commonly a palpable mass if advanced.
•
3. Ulcerative colitis
Typically causes bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, and starts from the rectum. Less likely in an
elderly patient with new onset symptoms.
•
4. Ischemic colitis
Presents with sudden onset of crampy abdominal pain (often LIF) and bloody diarrhea,
usually in patients with vascular disease or hypotensive episodes.
Summary:
Elderly patient + LIF pain, diarrhea, and past constipation = classic for sigmoid diverticulitis.

stem: A patient presented with lethargy, weakness and fever history. He had recurrent nasal bleeds. His RFTs were deranged. Urine analysis showed Blood 4+, Protein 1+.
explanation:
Correct Answer: 2. GPA (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis)
Explanation:
This patient presents with constitutional symptoms (fever, lethargy, weakness) along with:
•
ENT involvement → Recurrent nasal bleeds (epistaxis), highly suggestive of upper airway
granulomatous inflammation
•
Renal involvement:
o
Deranged renal function tests (RFTs)
o
Urinalysis: Blood 4+, Protein 1+ → indicates glomerulonephritis pattern
These findings together are classic for Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA), formerly known as
Wegener’s granulomatosis.
GPA Key Features:
System Typical Findings
ENT Nasal crusting, epistaxis, sinusitis, septal perforation
Lungs Nodules, cavitations, haemoptysis
Kidneys Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)
Blood tests Often c-ANCA positive (PR3 antibodies)
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
•
1. EGPA (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis)
More associated with asthma, eosinophilia, allergic features — not described here.
•
2. Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA)
Also causes glomerulonephritis, but ENT involvement is rare, and typically p-ANCA
positive.
•
3. SLE
Can cause glomerulonephritis and systemic symptoms, but would usually have additional
criteria (rash, joint pain, ANA positivity, etc.).
ENT bleeding is not typical.
•
4. Goodpasture's disease
Involves lungs and kidneys, but primarily presents with hemoptysis + glomerulonephritis,
not nasal bleeding or ENT disease.
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearl:
▪ ENT involvement + glomerulonephritis + constitutional symptoms = GPA, especially if c-
ANCA/PR3 positive.

stem: A 63 year old lady with pain in finger joints and thumb, worse with activity, better with rest. DIP joints involved. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: 1. Osteoarthritis
Explanation:
This is a classic presentation of osteoarthritis (OA) affecting the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint —
the base of the thumb, which is a very common site in elderly women.
Key Clinical Clues:
•
Age: 63-year-old woman — OA is more common with aging.
•
Joint pain worsens with activity, improves with rest → characteristic of mechanical (non-
inflammatory) arthritis
•
Site of pain: Base of thumb (1st CMC joint) — hallmark site for OA
•
X-ray:
o Joint space narrowing
o
Osteophyte formation (bone spurs)
o
These are classic radiological findings of OA
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
•
2. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
RA typically affects MCPs and PIPs, is bilateral and symmetrical, and has morning stiffness
30 min.
The base of the thumb (CMC joint) is not a typical early site of RA.
•
1. SLE
Joint involvement in SLE is typically non-erosive, migratory, and not limited to mechanical
symptoms like worsening with use.
•
2. Psoriatic arthritis
More likely to involve DIPs, nail pitting, dactylitis ("sausage digits"), and may have
asymmetrical involvement.
Base of thumb OA pattern is not typical.
Clinical Pearl:
In elderly women with activity-related thumb pain and x-ray evidence of joint space loss and
osteophytes, especially at the 1st CMC joint, think osteoarthritis
Feature of sub-acute thyroiditis were there (neck pain some days ago).
Anti-TPO were positive.
Most appropriate treatment?
1. Propranolol
2. Carbimazole
3. Propylthiouracil
4. Radioiodine
ANSWERS:
Propranolol
Correct Answer: 1. Propranolol
Explanation:
This patient has features suggestive of subacute thyroiditis (De Quervain’s thyroiditis):
•
History of neck pain a few days ago (often post-viral)
• Thyrotoxic symptoms likely present (tachycardia, tremor, palpitations, etc.)
•
Anti-TPO positive: While more typical of autoimmune thyroiditis (e.g., Hashimoto’s), mild
positivity can occur in subacute thyroiditis as well
Key Features of Subacute (De Quervain’s) Thyroiditis:
Feature Description
Painful neck Often preceded by a viral illness
Transient hyperthyroidism Due to release of preformed hormones
ESR/CRP ↑ Elevated inflammatory markers
Thyroid antibodies Usually negative, but mild anti-TPO may be present
Self-limiting May progress to hypothyroid phase, then recover
Best treatment: Propranolol
•
Used to control adrenergic symptoms of transient thyrotoxicosis (palpitations, tremor, anxiety)
•
Does not affect hormone synthesis, which is appropriate here since the hyperthyroidism is not
due to overproduction, but due to leakage of preformed hormones
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
• 2. Carbimazole
Antithyroid drug — inappropriate in subacute thyroiditis because there is no increased
synthesis of thyroid hormone
•
3. Propylthiouracil (PTU)
Same as above — ineffective in subacute thyroiditis
•
4. Radioiodine therapy
Not indicated for transient or inflammatory thyrotoxicosis
Reserved for Graves’ disease or toxic nodular goitre
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearl:
▪ In subacute thyroiditis, the thyrotoxic phase is treated symptomatically with beta-blockers
like propranolol, not with antithyroid drugs or radioiodine.

stem: Father had stress echo negative despite IHD risk factors. Daughter also had stress echo negative. Given disease prevalence is low in daughter's age group, what is affected?
options: Negative predictive value (NPV) — lower in low-prevalence population
explanation:
Correct Answer: NPV lower
Explanation:
You’re comparing two individuals with negative stress tests but different pre-test probabilities of
disease:
•
Father: Has multiple risk factors (e.g., smoking, known IHD) → high pre-test probability
•
Daughter: Has low risk factors → low pre-test probability
Both had a negative stress test — the question is about what statistical term applies when comparing
the father’s result to the daughter’s.
Negative Predictive Value (NPV):
•
NPV = Probability that someone with a negative test truly doesn’t have the disease
•
NPV depends on disease prevalence (or pre-test probability):
o
High pre-test probability → NPV decreases
o
Low pre-test probability → NPV increases
So:
•
The father (high risk) has a lower NPV → His negative test result is less reassuring
•
The daughter (low risk) has a higher NPV → Her negative result is more reliable
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
•
PPV (Positive Predictive Value)
Not relevant — both had negative test results.
•
Sensitivity / Specificity
These are test characteristics and do not change between patients — they are independent
of disease prevalence
Summary:
The correct statistical term when comparing the father's negative result (high risk) to the daughter's (low
risk) is:
▪ NPV is lower in the father.
Effect of Disease Prevalence on PPV and NPV
Disease
Prevalence
Positive Predictive
Value (PPV)
Negative
Predictive Value
(NPV)
Explanation

prevalence

Few true positives → most positive results
are false positives
Moderate
prevalence

PPV and NPV both reflect balanced
predictive accuracy

more likely true; negative results less
reassuring
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Implication:
•
In high-risk (high prevalence) populations:
o
A negative test is less reliable → NPV is lower
o
A positive test is more reliable → PPV is higher
•
In low-risk (low prevalence) populations:
o A negative test is very reassuring → NPV is high
o
A positive test may be a false positive → PPV is low
Summary Rule of Thumb:
Prevalence ↑ → PPV ↑, NPV ↓
Prevalence ↓ → PPV ↓, NPV ↑

stem: Battery manufacturing worker 45 years complaints of abdominal pain and blood picture HB:10 MCV :78 What most common poisoning occurred?
explanation:
Correct Answer: 1. Lead
Explanation:
This is a classic case of occupational lead poisoning, particularly in a battery manufacturing worker,
which is a well-known high-risk industry for lead exposure.
Key Clinical Clues:
•
Occupation: Battery manufacturing = high lead exposure
•
Symptoms: Abdominal pain (classic “lead colic”)
• Bloods:
o
Hb: 10 g/dL → anemia
o
MCV: 78 fL → microcytic anemia
These findings point toward lead toxicity causing:
• Microcytic, hypochromic anemia
•
Basophilic stippling (may be seen on blood film)
Abdominal pain
•
Neurological symptoms (e.g., wrist drop in chronic cases)
Mechanism:
•
Lead inhibits δ-ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis → resulting in
sideroblastic-like anemia
•
Also causes bone marrow suppression and neuropathy
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
•
2. Lithium
Used in bipolar disorder — toxicity causes tremor, ataxia, renal issues, not anemia or
abdominal pain.
•
3. Silicon (silica)
Causes pulmonary fibrosis (silicosis), not anemia or abdominal pain. No hematologic
toxicity.
Summary:
Battery worker + abdominal pain + microcytic anemia = classic for lead poisoning

stem: A man tooth extraction bleeding occurred PT = 12 APTT = 98 Which factor deficiency?
explanation:
Explanation:
This patient has prolonged bleeding after a minor procedure (tooth extraction) with:
•
Normal PT = 12 (normal range ≈11–14 seconds)
•
Prolonged APTT = 98 (very elevated)
Interpreting Coagulation Tests:
Test Pathway Tested Prolonged When
PT Extrinsic + common Factor VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen
APTT Intrinsic + common Factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II
Key Analysis:
•
Normal PT → extrinsic and common pathways are intact
•
Prolonged APTT only → defect in intrinsic pathway (Factors VIII, IX, XI, or XII)
•
Severe prolongation of APTT + bleeding tendency strongly suggests:
o
Factor VIII deficiency = Haemophilia A
o
(Factor IX = Haemophilia B is also possible, but less likely with such marked APTT
elevation)
•
Factor XII deficiency can cause very prolonged APTT, but does NOT cause bleeding.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
•
A) Factor V
Affects both PT and APTT → would prolong both
•
B) Factor VI
Does not exist — obsolete/incorrect option
•
D) Factor X
Common pathway → would prolong both PT and APTT
E) Factor XII
Prolongs APTT but does not cause bleeding
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearl:
• Isolated prolonged APTT + bleeding = think intrinsic pathway defect → most likely Factor
VIII (Haemophilia A)

stem: A patient is started on carbimazole for hyperthyroidism. Which investigation must be monitored regularly?
explanation:
Correct Answer: FBC (Full Blood Count)
Explanation:
Carbimazole is an antithyroid medication used to treat hyperthyroidism, particularly in Graves' disease
and toxic nodular goitre.
One of the most important and potentially life-threatening side effects of carbimazole is:
Agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia)
This is why FBC (Full Blood Count) monitoring is crucial.
What to Monitor in Patients on Carbimazole:
Parameter Reason for Monitoring
FBC To detect agranulocytosis early (look for ↓ WBC, especially neutrophils)
Thyroid function tests
(TFTs)
To monitor response to therapy (TSH, free T4)
Clinical vigilance
Patients should be told to report sore throat, fever, or mouth ulcers
immediately
Routine repeat FBCs Not always needed unless symptoms suggest possible agranulocytosis
MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearl:
▪ In patients on carbimazole, fever or sore throat should prompt immediate FBC to rule out
agranulocytosis — and the drug should be stopped immediately if confirmed.

stem: Patient with bilateral flank pain and haematuria 2 months after sore throat. Urine 3+ blood. Which blood test is abnormal?
A child presents 2 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection with haematuria, oedema and hypertension. Which complement component is characteristically reduced?
Patient with gait abnormalities, urinary incontinence and dementia (NPH triad). What intervention relieves symptoms?
explanation:
Correct Answer: CSF drain
Explanation:
The classic triad of:
1. Gait abnormalities (e.g. magnetic gait or shuffling)
2. Urinary incontinence
3. Cognitive decline (dementia)
is characteristic of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH).
NPH Key Features:
Feature Explanation
Gait disturbance Often the earliest and most prominent symptom
Incontinence Usually urge incontinence due to frontal lobe dysfunction
Dementia Frontal-subcortical dementia with apathy, slowed thinking
Imaging Enlarged ventricles (hydrocephalus) with normal CSF pressure
Why CSF Drain Is the Correct Intervention:
•
A large-volume lumbar puncture (CSF drain) serves two purposes:
o
Diagnostic: Improvement after drainage supports NPH
o Therapeutic: Temporarily relieves symptoms by reducing CSF volume
•
If symptoms improve, the patient is likely to benefit from a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt,
which is the definitive treatment.
Why Acetazolamide Is Incorrect:
Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production.
•
It is used in Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH), where CSF pressure is elevated, not in
NPH where pressure is normal.
Summary:
In a patient with the classic NPH triad (gait, incontinence, dementia), a CSF drain is the most appropriate
and effective intervention to both diagnose and relieve symptoms.

stem: An HIV patient with CD4 < 60 presents with homonymous hemianopia. CT scan shows multiple low-enhancing lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)
Explanation:
This is a classic presentation of PML in an advanced HIV patient:
Key Clinical Clues:
•
HIV patient with CD4 < 60 → severe immunosuppression
•
CT scan: Multiple low-attenuation (hypodense), non-enhancing lesions
•
Neurological deficit: Homonymous hemianopia → suggests posterior brain involvement,
often parieto-occipital
About PML (Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy):
• Cause: Reactivation of JC virus in immunocompromised individuals
•
Pathophysiology: Demyelination due to JC virus attacking oligodendrocytes
•
Neuroimaging (better seen on MRI than CT):
o
Multiple asymmetric white matter lesions
o
No mass effect
o No contrast enhancement (or very faint)
•
Clinical signs:
o
Focal neurological deficits (e.g. hemianopia, hemiparesis, aphasia)
o No fever or systemic signs
Differentials (and why less likely here):
•
Cerebral toxoplasmosis:
Causes ring-enhancing lesions with mass effect, more common when CD4 <100, but
typically causes headache, seizures, focal deficits, not isolated homonymous hemianopia.
•
Primary CNS lymphoma:
Usually solitary or few lesions, often enhancing, and more mass effect.
•
CMV encephalitis:
Presents with confusion, fever, and retinitis, not focal deficits with low-attenuation lesions.
Summary:
In an HIV patient with CD4 <60, focal neurological deficits (e.g. homonymous hemianopia), and
multiple low-attenuation lesions on imaging without enhancement or mass effect, the most likely
diagnosis is PML due to JC virus reactivation.

stem: Old man good comprehension and fluent sometimes problem with repetition Pattern of aphasia?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B) Conductive aphasia
Explanation:
This patient has the following language features:
•
Good comprehension
• Fluent speech
•
Problem with repetition
This triad points directly to conductive aphasia.
Conductive Aphasia: Key Features:
Feature Status
Comprehension Preserved
Fluency Fluent speech
Repetition Impaired
•
This is classic for Conductive Aphasia, which results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus, the
white matter tract connecting Broca’s area (speech production) and Wernicke’s area (language
comprehension).Patients can understand and speak fluently, but cannot repeat phrases
accurately.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
•
A) Wernicke’s aphasia
Fluent speech, but poor comprehension and poor repetition
• C) Receptive aphasia
Synonym for Wernicke’s → again, poor comprehension
•
D) Expressive aphasia
Another term for Broca’s aphasia → non-fluent speech, good comprehension, poor
repetition
Summary:
Fluent speech + good comprehension + impaired repetition = Conductive aphasia (lesion in arcuate
fasciculus)
Aphasia Patterns Comparison:
Aphasia Type Fluent? Comprehension Repetition
Wernicke’s (A) Fluent Impaired Impaired
Conductive (B) Fluent Preserved Impaired
Receptive (C)* Fluent Impaired Impaired
Expressive (D) Non-fluent Preserved Impaired
*Note: "Receptive aphasia" is another term for Wernicke’s aphasia.
Summary:
Fluent speech + good comprehension + impaired repetition = Conductive aphasia → damage to
arcuate fasciculus.

stem: A 23 year old patient presented with 200 ml of recent hemoptysis. He had a history of Cystic fibrosis and recurrent lung infections. He is known to be a colonizer of pseudomonas. What is the most likely reason for his hemoptysis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Bronchiectasis
Explanation:
This 23-year-old patient with:
• Cystic fibrosis (CF)
•
Recurrent lung infections
•
Colonization with Pseudomonas
•
Presents with significant hemoptysis (200 mL)
is demonstrating a classic complication of CF-related bronchiectasis.
Why Bronchiectasis Is the Most Likely Cause:
•
CF commonly leads to bronchiectasis, particularly in early adulthood.
•
Bronchiectasis causes:
o
Chronic airway inflammation
o
Destruction of bronchial walls
o
Abnormal, dilated airways that are prone to:
▪
Recurrent infections (especially with Pseudomonas)
▪
Erosion of bronchial arteries, leading to hemoptysis
• Hemoptysis in CF is often due to exacerbations of bronchiectasis or rupture of hypertrophied
bronchial arteries.
Why Other Options Are Less Likely:
•
ABPA (Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis)
Can occur in CF but typically presents with:
o Wheezing
o
Eosinophilia
Elevated IgE
o
Central bronchiectasis
Hemoptysis is not the primary feature, and there’s no mention of asthma-like
symptoms or eosinophilia here.
•
Foreign body
Would be unusual in a young adult with CF
Causes sudden-onset localized wheeze or unilateral changes, and is not consistent with
chronic lung colonization and prior infections.
Summary:
In a CF patient with recurrent infections and pseudomonas colonization, bronchiectasis is the most
likely cause of hemoptysis due to airway damage and fragile bronchial vessels.

Age Group / Context Common Causes Key Features

• Foreign body aspiration- Lower
respiratory tract infection-

wheeze; infection-related signs;
history of chronic disease

colonization (CF), cavitation (TB),
recurrent infections

carcinoma (esp. smokers)- Bronchitis-
Pulmonary embolism
Systemic symptoms (TB or cancer),
pleuritic chest pain (PE), fever and
sputum (bronchitis)

(pulmonary edema)- Anticoagulant-

patients

high IgE if ABPA present

hemorrhage on imaging

Diagnostic Tips:
•
Massive hemoptysis (>200–600 mL/day): Think bronchiectasis, TB, or lung cancer.
•
Recurrent hemoptysis + chronic infection: Think bronchiectasis (e.g., CF).
•
Hemoptysis + hematuria: Think vasculitis or Goodpasture’s.
•
Pleuritic chest pain + hemoptysis + tachycardia: Think pulmonary embolism.

stem: CKD patient having following parameters Ca decreased PTH Increased Vit D increased What’s the cause of hyperphosphatemia?
explanation:
Correct Answer: 3) 1,25-hydroxylase deficiency
Explanation:
In chronic kidney disease (CKD), mineral and bone disorders are common due to disturbed calcium,
phosphate, and vitamin D metabolism.
Key Laboratory Findings Given:
•
↓ Calcium
• ↑ PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
•
↑ Phosphate (hyperphosphatemia)
•
↑ Vitamin D (but likely refers to 25(OH)D — the inactive form)
Pathophysiology in CKD:
•
The kidney normally converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (the active
form) via the enzyme 1α-hydroxylase.
•
In CKD, the activity of 1α-hydroxylase is reduced → low 1,25(OH)₂D, despite normal or high
25(OH)D.
•
This leads to:
o
Reduced calcium absorption from the gut → ↓ calcium
o
↑ PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
o
↑ phosphate due to decreased renal excretion
This is best explained by 1,25-hydroxylase deficiency (i.e., impaired renal conversion due to CKD).
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
•
1. Primary hyperparathyroidism
Would show ↑ calcium and ↓ phosphate, not the findings here.
•
2. 25-hydroxylase deficiency
Would cause low total vitamin D (25(OH)D), but this is reported high/normal in the
question.
Hyperthyroidism
May cause mild hypercalcemia due to bone turnover, but not this pattern of findings.
Summary:
In a CKD patient with low calcium, high PTH, high phosphate, and normal/high 25(OH)D, the most
likely cause is deficiency of 1α-hydroxylase, i.e.,1,25-hydroxylase deficiency.

stem: Most common complications of inhaled steroid in COPD patient?
explanation:
Correct Answer: Pneumonia
Explanation:
In patients with COPD, inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) such as fluticasone or budesonide are commonly
used in combination with bronchodilators to reduce exacerbations in patients with moderate-to-severe
disease or frequent exacerbators.
However, ICS use in COPD is associated with an increased risk of certain complications.
Most Common and Clinically Significant Complication:
• Pneumonia is the most common and clinically significant complication of inhaled
corticosteroids in COPD.
o
ICS suppress local airway immunity
o
Increases risk of bacterial pneumonia, especially in patients with:
▪
Severe COPD
▪ Older age
▪
Prior pneumonic episodes
Why Other Options Are Less Likely in COPD:
•
Skin bruising (dermal thinning)
Can occur, especially with long-term ICS use, but less common and less severe than
pneumonia in COPD patients.
•
Osteoporosis
Systemic corticosteroids cause this more commonly; ICS may have a small effect, but it's not
the most common complication.
Summary:
In COPD patients, the most common and important complication of inhaled corticosteroids is:
Pneumonia

stem: A patient presented to the emergency department with metastatic cancer came to disorientation. Her family knows he passed a few days. BP 90/70 and SPO2 91% and hemoptysis occurred blood 200ml DNR was signed Most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Key Features from the Scenario:
•
Patient with metastatic cancer
• Presents with:
o
Disorientation (suggesting terminal agitation or delirium)
o
Low BP (90/70) and hypoxia (SpO₂ 91%)
o
Hemoptysis (200 mL)
o
DNR order signed
• Prognosis: terminal (family expects death within days)
Why Midazolam is the most appropriate:
•
Disorientation + terminal illness suggests agitation, terminal delirium, or restlessness,
common in the dying phase.
•
Midazolam is the first-line medication in palliative care to manage:
o
Terminal agitation
o
Anxiety
o
Dyspnea-related distress
• Rapid onset and can be administered subcutaneously or intravenously, ideal in emergency
palliative settings.
•
Prioritizes comfort-focused care, in line with the DNR and expected death.
Why other options are inappropriate:
Option Reason
1. Red cell
count
Not useful in end-of-life care. Would not change management. Blood loss is palliative
concern, not for active intervention.
2. Nebulized
0.9% NaCl
Sometimes used to loosen secretions or help with breathlessness, but not the primary
treatment for agitation or distress. Provides minimal benefit in terminal hemoptysis or
delirium.
Palliative Approach:
Focus on comfort, dignity, and symptom control. In this context, Midazolam is the correct and
compassionate next step.
Final answer: Midazolam

stem: Post-chemotherapy patient: painful rash starting as vesicles progressing to pustules bilaterally on legs, then body and abdomen. Pyrexial. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Key Clinical Clues:
•
Post-chemotherapy (strong clue for immunosuppression and drug-related complications)
•
Painful rash, initially vesicular, progressing to pustules
•
Distribution: both legs → then generalized to body and abdomen bilaterally
•
Associated with fever (pyrexia)
Reasoning for Diagnosis:
➤ Drug reaction is most likely because:
•
Chemotherapy is a common trigger of drug-induced skin reactions, especially toxic erythema,
SJS/TEN, or morbilliform rash.
•
Vesicles evolving into pustules with widespread distribution, often accompanied by fever, strongly
suggests a systemic drug reaction.
• Widespread rash with mucosal involvement or pain is typical of severe drug eruptions (e.g.,
SJS, TEN, or DRESS).
Timing post-chemotherapy fits with delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
Why other options are less likely:
Option Reason it’s less likely
A) Bacterial
Fasciitis
Localized, rapidly progressive soft tissue infection; usually unilateral, extremely painful,
not vesicular-pustular. Would expect crepitus, swelling, systemic toxicity, and not
widespread symmetrical rash.
B) Pemphigus
vulgaris
Autoimmune blistering disorder; vesicles are typically flaccid, rupture easily, and
involve mucosa (oral lesions), and it’s not pustular, nor commonly linked directly to
chemo. Chronic course.
Summary:
A widespread painful rash following chemotherapy, evolving from vesicles to pustules with fever, is
most consistent with a drug reaction (likely severe). Always consider SJS/TEN or DRESS in this context.
Final Answer: C) Drug reaction

stem: A patient is in the terminal stage of cancer. Unable to eat or swallow. Noisy respiratory sounds are present (death rattle). What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Key Clinical Features:
•
Terminal cancer patient
•
Unable to eat or swallow (dysphagia)
• Noisy respiratory sounds → suggests terminal respiratory secretions ("death rattle")
•
End-of-life context (comfort care focus)
Why Glycopyrronium is the correct choice:
•
Glycopyrronium is an anticholinergic agent used to reduce respiratory secretions in terminal
patients.
•
Noisy breathing at the end of life is usually caused by pooling of secretions the patient can no
longer clear due to decreased consciousness and swallowing.
•
Glycopyrronium dries up these secretions, improving comfort and dignity, not prolonging life.
Why IV Saline is not appropriate:
•
In the dying phase, hydration does not improve symptoms and may worsen secretions, cause
pulmonary edema, or prolong dying uncomfortably.
•
The focus is not life prolongation, but symptom control and comfort.
•
IV fluids have no role in managing noisy respiration in terminal care.
Summary:
In end-of-life care, noisy respiration from secretions is best managed with glycopyrronium, which helps
dry secretions and provides comfort. IV fluids may actually worsen the situation.
Final Answer: 2) Glycopyrronium bromide

stem: A 28 year woman with 8 weeks of pregnancy. She has asthma & took ICS & LABA/SABA. But after becoming pregnant she kept hold of all her medication & came to you for advice. What would be the best treatment option?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
28-year-old woman, 8 weeks pregnant
•
Known asthmatic – previously on ICS + LABA/SABA
•
Stopped all medications due to pregnancy
•
Seeks advice on what to do
Rationale for the Correct Answer:
➤ Asthma in Pregnancy:
•
Uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy is more dangerous than most asthma medications.
•
Poor control leads to:
o
Maternal hypoxia
o
Fetal growth restriction
o
Preterm birth
o
Stillbirth
➤ Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) and LABA/SABA:
•
Considered safe in pregnancy
•
ICS (e.g., budesonide) are first-line maintenance
•
LABAs (e.g., salmeterol, formoterol) are used if asthma is not controlled on ICS alone
•
SABA (e.g., salbutamol) is used for relief of symptoms
➤ Guideline Recommendation (e.g., BTS/SIGN, GINA):
•
Do not stop asthma medications during pregnancy
• Continue or restart previous effective regimen
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
Option Reason
a. Give only ICS
Not enough if she previously needed ICS + LABA/SABA. Stepping down risks loss of
control.
b. Give only LABA
LABAs must never be used without ICS due to increased risk of asthma-related
death.
c. Give
montelukast
Not first-line. Used only if patient was already on it and it helped. Limited safety
data in pregnancy.
Summary:
Asthma control is essential in pregnancy. Inhalers (ICS, LABA, SABA) are safe and should be continued or
restarted if previously effective. The benefits outweigh theoretical risks.
Final Answer: d. Start previous treatment

stem: Asthma new diagnosis done. ICS started. But after 6 month condition not improving. H/o eczema/hay fever. What is the next appropriate step?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:
•
Asthma newly diagnosed
•
ICS already started
•
No improvement after 6 months
•
History of atopy (eczema/hay fever — supports asthma diagnosis)
Explanation:
Before escalating treatment in asthma, always assess three things first:
1. Inhaler technique – Incorrect technique is a very common cause of poor asthma control.
2. Adherence to medication – Has the patient been taking it as prescribed?
3. Trigger exposure or comorbidities – Ongoing allergen exposure, reflux, smoking, etc.
So, the first and most appropriate next step is:
• Check inhaler technique
Why other options are less appropriate at this stage:
•
a. Increase ICS dose
Not appropriate before confirming adherence and technique. Step-up therapy is only
recommended after confirming proper usage.
•
c. Add montelukast
Montelukast is an add-on but not first-line at this stage. Typically considered for exercise-
induced asthma or in children, or if there's ongoing allergic rhinitis.
•
d. Add LABA
Also part of step-up therapy but only after confirming poor control despite correct
technique and adherence. LABA should never be used without ICS.
